This is rather a strange procedure,
and I suggest that this motion has no right to be put at all, at least without notice. So far as we are concerned we have never seen these bills. They may be unopposed; I do not know anything about them, but certainly I question the desirability of this procedure.

AFFECTING FOREIGN NATIONALS DOMICILED IN CANADA
speechtext:
1.	Has any non-British country the right and power to enforce within Canada, acts, decrees, regulations, etc., made or issued by the said non-British government, ordering its nationals domiciled in Canada to undertake compulsory service in the armed forces of the said government?
2.	If so, under what authority?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: AFFECTING FOREIGN NATIONALS DOMICILED IN CANADA
speechtext:
I should like to say just a word in regard to this question, to point out to the hon. gentleman who has asked it that the question really solicits a legal opinion. If we were to hold strictly to the rules and not establish a precedent which might be very embarrassing I think I would have to ask him to allow me to decline to answer the question. Questions on the order paper are for the purpose of eliciting facts, but not legal opinions or expressions of opinion with respect to theories or other matters. However this is a subject of general interest, and I believe it might be advisable on the whole to clarify what seems to be a matter of doubt in the minds of some. Therefore I shall give an answer. I should like it to be understood however that it must not be cited hereafter as a precedent for giving legal opinions. The answer to the question is as follows:
No non-British country has the right and power to enforce within Canada acts, decrees, regulations, et cetera, made or issued by its government, ordering its nationals domiciled in Canada to undertake compulsory service in its armed forces.
A foreign government, which has a legal system imposing compulsory military service on its nationals abroad, can, under existing international practice, provide for calling them up. Its representatives can bring the call to the attention of the nationals. They cannot exercise any compulsion within Canada in order to induce them to respond to the call.
The national of the foreign government can refuse to respond to the call, without incurring any penalties within this country. On the other hand he will not be able to embark on a 14873-155
ship flying the flag of his home country or enter its territories without subjecting himself to prosecution in his own country.
Under the Foreign Forces Order 1941, the forces of certain allied countries are enabled to maintain their own discipline and internal administration. For such purposes, they can arrest members of their own forces within this country and can call upon Canadian civilian and military police to assist them in maintaining their own discipline. The provisions of the order, however, make it clear that the measures of compulsion do not apply to a person who, while in Canada, has been called up for service under the law of a foreign power and who has failed to comply with such call or to be enrolled in its service.

subtopic: SUSPENSION OF STANDING ORDER 28 THIS DAY TO PERMIT DEBATE ON MOTION OF MR. ILSLEY FOR COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if the debate of yesterday is to be proceeded with, a motion will be required, and will have to have the unanimous approval of the house. I gather from reading Hansard that last night there was some doubt in the mind of the minister as to whether we could proceed without a motion. He was of the opinion that we did not require one. However standing order 28 is as follows:
On Thursdays and Fridays when the order of the day is called for the house to go into committee of supply, or of ways and means, Mr. Speaker shall leave the chair without putting any question, provided that, except by the unanimous consent of the house, the estimates of each department shall be first taken up on a day other than Thursday or Friday.

Supply-State oj Agriculture

The motion I would move so as to enable the house to continue the debate on the amendment to go into supply, if there is no objection to continuing that debate, would be the following:
That the provision of standing order 28, in relation to Mr. Speaker leaving the chair without putting any question, be suspended this day, in order to allow debate on the proposed amendment and subamendment to the motion that the house be resolved into committee of supply.
If there is any objection to that motion, of course the house will not be able to proceed.

subtopic: SUSPENSION OF STANDING ORDER 28 THIS DAY TO PERMIT DEBATE ON MOTION OF MR. ILSLEY FOR COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY

I take it that the motion now before the house regularizes that position.

subtopic: SUSPENSION OF STANDING ORDER 28 THIS DAY TO PERMIT DEBATE ON MOTION OF MR. ILSLEY FOR COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
subsubtopic: AGRICULTURE-AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the debate was adjourned last night I was referring to the proposal that had been made by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) to pay half the transportation costs on a certain quantity of wheat from western Canada to the eastern provinces. Some hon. members have questioned the figures I quoted, and with that in mind I have gone into the matter further.
I stated last night that in certain quarters of Quebec wheat retailed at SI .60, and that the same wheat was sold off the farm in western Canada for as little as 50 cents. Because those figures were questioned I sought further information, and I have gathered from experts that most of the wheat sold privately on western farms did not bring to the western farmer more than 50 cents. On the other hand when the eastern farmer wants to buy wheat for feeding purposes the cost is considerable. I have learned that the wholesale price of No. 1 northern in car lots is 86 cents. When I stated that $1.60 was paid

I was referring to cleaned wheat sold at retail in most parts of Quebec at $1.60. That is the explanation I give in connection with the figures which have been questioned.
Last night I referred to the attitude taken by the Premier and Minister of Agriculture of Quebec, the Hon. Adelard Godbout. I stated that while I have the greatest confidence in the federal Minister of Agriculture -and I indicated yesterday what I thought of him-I had just as much confidence in our friend, the Premier of Quebec, who is an expert in agricultural matters. For many years Mr. Godbout has held the portfolio of minister of agriculture. I know that he is now devoting all his energy toward bringing about betterment and advancement of sane agricultural conditions in Quebec.
I knew, too, that Mr. Godbout in Quebec was assisted by a group of experts, headed by his acting deputy minister, Mr. Adrien Morin, another brilliant technician in agriculture.
I could scarcely believe the premier would let pass an opportunity to benefit Quebec or the farmers of that province. I could not believe that he would fail to avail himself of these 'advantages. As I said yesterday, I went to the source and got some information as to how these negotiations had been carried on. What happened in connection with this proposal is this:	The federal offer
was that the federal government would pay 50 per cent of transportation costs, the provinces would pay 25 per cent and the railways 25 per cent. I understand a meeting was held at Toronto at which were present the provincial ministers of agriculture from eastern Canada and the chairmen of the two great railway systems. After considerable discussion the latter refused to reduce their freight rates to the extent of 25 per cent of the costs of transportation.
The provinces were then put in the position of having to consider paying fifty per cent of the cost of transporting the wheat. That would involve a considerable sum of money. At the same time there was some indication that the price of wheat was going up. The reduction in the cost of transport would have benefited the eastern farmers, but this would have been wiped out almost entirely by the increase in the price in western Canada. The Quebec department of agriculture had to consider this matter before they decided upon expending a considerable amount of money. When I said that the cost of this proposal was high, I meant that the operation of the plan would have necessitated quite an army of employees; and that above the cost of transportation itself.

Supply-State of Agriculture
It would have been necessary to take stock before the plan was put into operation, and another inventory might have been necessary after July 1 when the offer lapses. I understand that the Quebec authorities have examined the situation with a view to bringing help and relief to the class of farmers which would have benefited from this. According to the figures I have, almost ninety-five per cent of the Quebec farmers produce some milk. The provincial government decided that instead of accepting the plan to reduce the cost of transportation, they would give a bonus on cheese of two cents per pound. This provincial bonus was to be in addition to the federal bonus, and it was announced by the provincial minister of agriculture. Final steps have not been taken, but this announcement has been made by the premier and minister of agriculture. This will really help the farmer much more than would have been the case if a reduction in cost of transportation of feedstuffs had been brought about.
The provincial department of agriculture felt that the farmers in each community should be encouraged to grow all the grain they needed for feed purposes. They would then have to buy only the concentrates which they needed. I then realized that the Quebec government acted wisely and in the interests of Quebec farmers. While the federal proposal might seem to be attractive, the fact is that the rise in prices in western Canada, while they benefited the western farmer, prevented a benefit to the eastern consumer. There was also the high cost of operating the plan to be considered. Instead of this, the Quebec government decided to pay a bonus on cheese which will involve the expenditure this year of over $650,000.
Some hon. members have referred to the reduction which has been made in the estimates of the Department of Agriculture. I think it is most regrettable that these reductions have had to be made. I referred to this when I spoke on the address. However, I understand that the reductions have been made -with the greatest care. One of the reductions is in connection with grants to exhibitions and provincial and local fairs. These grants are an incentive to better farm production, but from conversations wdiich I have had with chairmen of cooperatives in my constituency I am led to believe that this expenditure is not indispensable. It is a good thing, but it is not indispensable and we should not complain too much over what has been done. However. T repeat that it is not wise economy to curtail the services provided by this department to farmers throughout Canada. It is important to help to save the world
14873-155i
from barbarism, but it is also important to feed Great Britain, not only with our wheat but with meat, cheese and butter. One thing we can do is to improve our production. That cannot be done by curtailing the services offered by this department. I think it would be better to try to cut expenses elsewhere rather than to reduce the help given to farmers.
I understand that there has been a reduction in the vote for demonstration farms, but we are told that this reduction will not mean that these farms will not be carried on. However, the experience in my own constituency is that this work is being curtailed.
Another point is the accreditation of herds. Now is the time to help our farmers, and yet this work is being curtailed because of a reduction in the estimates. One of our aims should be to help our cattle growers improve their herds in order that they may be able to compete with the Argentine and other south American countries on the British market.
Another matter discussed frequently in Quebec is the minimum price on butter. I know the minister is giving considerable attention to this problem. Opinions vary considerably as to what the price should be, and the representations which have been made to me may be based on too high a price. I state again that I am not an expert, and I do not want to pose as one. It is claimed that a price of between 33 and 35 cents per pound would be fair. Our farmers have had a number of lean years during which they had little chance to earn a living; would we be acting justly and equitably if we prevented them at a time like this from taking advantage of higher markets? Would it not be better to give them a chance and fix a reasonable limit?
I am told that farm products are still being imported from the United States even though these importations were supposed to be curtailed. There may be some reason for bringing in seasonable vegetables, but the importation of new potatoes in the winter and spring is an unwarranted luxury. It would be better to prevent the importation of sueh luxuries than to stop the bringing in of certain farm necessities, such as kerosene stoves and other things of the kind which have been banned from Canada. It has been said that these articles are manufactured in Canada, but I am told that there is a shortage at the present time. The local companies are not manufacturing these articles in sufficient volume or at a price low enough to compare with the previous prices of the United States products. Many of these articles are used mainly on farms or by small wage earners.
Supply-State of Agriculture

There should be more cooperation between the officials of the federal Department of Agriculture and the provincial department in order that the fate of our agricultural class may be bettered. I am sure that if the officials of the two departments get together, good results will ensue. Research should be carried on for opening up new avenues of production, in agriculture, and the experts of the federal department may be able to help those of the provincial departments. The culture of finer tobaccos has been started in Quebec and this might be benefited by research carried on by the federal government. The same is true of the production of flax and of sugar beets. There are many avenues of production which might prove profitable to the small farmer of Quebec.
Another matter which is mentioned quite often in our district is the establishment of tuberculosis-free areas. I understand that this work has been quite extensive and that at the present time more than half of the province of Quebec is under the plan. I believe that quite a larger number of farmers have agreed to come under the plan. I understand that the plan works out in this way. The provincial officials get the signatures of the farmers in a certain area who want to come in under the plan, and once a sufficient number of signatures has been obtained the federal authorities are asked to put the plan into operation. I understand that at the present time quite a number of farmers have signified a desire to come under the plan and that there are quite a number of areas that could be covered. But actually the plan seems to have been suspended for the duration of the war, and the result is that many parts of the province of Quebec do not get as sanitary a milk supply as they would if these tuberculosis-free areas had been established in the districts agreed upon.
Another point that has been made to me in connection with cooperation between the provincial and federal governments concerns the contagious abortion in cattle. Closer cooperation is considered important in many quarters also for a stricter application of the regulations concerning the moving from one province to another of infected animals.
That brings me, Mr. Speaker, to a question I hesitate to mention, and that is the qualifications of the federal officers appointed by the Department of Agriculture to administer these regulations in the province of Quebec. I know this is a delicate question, but in the general interest we might as well face it. Up to now there have been frequent complaints in many parts of the province of Quebec that the federal officers having to do

with the slaughtering of infected animals do not speak the French language. It is true that the farmer gets compensation when an animal is slaughtered, but it covers only part of his loss, and the blow is not softened at all when the official with whom he is dealing cannot make himself understood in a language the farmer understands but has to explain things through a third person. I again say that I appreciate that this is a delicate question, but I think this is the proper time to mention it because we all want national unity, particularly at this time when we are asking our people to defend our country and they are often treated as if they did not belong to that country. I am sure it will be realized how difficult it is for the people of our province when the officials of the federal government with whom they are dealing cannot make themselves understood. I am sure that all members from the province of Quebec desire to help the government all they can but they should at least be also given help by the government in doing away with these irritating annoyances and this is one place where help should be given. I shall not trespass, concerning bilingualism, upon any other field than agriculture to-day, but this is a case where the point is of great importance. I know the fault is not with the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) himself but rather with some of his officials who do not give him proper advice.
May I be permitted to mention an incident that occurred a few years ago, when I was told by a perfect stranger that there was a meeting of a certain number of officials and the question of a bilingual appointment in the province of Quebec came up. One of the officials present said, "My people say that we cannot find any French-speaking person in the province of Quebec with the necessaiy qualifications to carry on that work". I am told that the Minister of Agriculture in this government was present and that he said to those present: "Well, you might inquire further because I have had a similar experience. I was told by my department one day that a man of those qualifications and experience could not be found in the province of Quebec, but I went to the Sherbrooke fair and talked to a man there who knew his job thoroughly. I spoke to him afterwards and asked him, 'Are you from the province of Quebec?' 'Yes', he replied. Then I asked him if he was a graduate of Macdonald college, and he told me that he was a graduate of St. Anne de la Pocatiere." Then the Minister of Agriculture went on to say to these officials: "Do not make the same mistake I made then by listening to my advisers, because I really think

Supply-State oj Agriculture
you will be able to find a man in the province of Quebec with the necessary qualifications for the position."
I mention this incident to show the goodwill of the minister and the efforts that he has made at all times. But I must say that the results are not always satisfactory. At the present time we are asking the farmers to spend more and more to improve their herds, and I do think we should appoint officials who can speak the language the farmers understand. It does not put the farmer in any better humour to be told, by an official who cannot make himself understood, to carry out orders. Particularly at this time when it is essential to win cooperation our people in the province of Quebec feel that they are treated so strangely by some of the officials that they begin to wonder whether they really belong to the country. I say that with all due respect to the minister, because as I said before I know his own personal goodwill. I mention the point because it has been brought to my attention, particularly in this matter of tuberculosis-free areas, and because I believe it is of great importance. If this work of inspection is to be resumed I trust that officials will be appointed as inspectors who can speak the language of the people with whom they are dealing, so that they can gain their goodwill and friendly cooperation, which is much better than dictating to them, in a language they do not understand, what they must do.
May I also suggest that the minister and his experts study the possibilities of applying to Canada the Farm Surplus Disposal Act which has been applied in many parts of the United States. I am not sufficiently acquainted with all its details to impose upon hon. members a description of it, but I have read a good deal about it, and where it has been put into operation it seems to have helped considerably. I suggest that further study be given to that act with a view to helping our farmers dispose of their products and at the same time helping to relieve unemployed people by giving them farm products at a nominal price.
In conclusion may I repeat that we in the east are not envious of the western farmers. Kipling's words, "East is east and west is west and never the twain shall meet," should not apply in our country. Rather the east and the west should go along hand in hand, understanding one another better and progressing together. Our agricultural economy should be nationally adjusted and geared in such a way that it may help the country towards a better and a more prosperous future.

subtopic: SUSPENSION OF STANDING ORDER 28 THIS DAY TO PERMIT DEBATE ON MOTION OF MR. ILSLEY FOR COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
subsubtopic: AGRICULTURE-AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, to my mind the amendment moved by the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefen-baker) does not in any sense amount to a want of confidence motion. The motion was brought forward with the best of good-will in order that a thorough discussion might take place of the agricultural problems of this country, and the discussion we have had so far has served a very useful purpose.
I shall come shortly to the subamendment. I should like to draw the attention of the house to a few remarks which were made the other day by the hon. member for Renfrew North (Mr. Warren). He said:
It is the easiest thing in the world to create a spirit of self-pity in any class. You can create it among farmers or labouring men, and it is one of the worst diseases with which any individual or class could be afflicted. Cancer is bad, but I believe that self-pity is responsible for more unhappiness and discontent than ever could be the case with cancer.
I do not think that that statement was necessary. Back in 1939, as reported on page 2895 of Hansard of that year, we had a discussion in this house about transient unemployed. The point is that at that time we had to face the facts with respect to transient unemployed; and the hon. member for Renfrew North then said:
What gets under my skin is this, that there is a deliberate attempt as I see it on the part of certain members to encourage our young Canadian men to rely wholly on the government for their livelihood.
Well, Mr. Speaker, that was not so at that time. We had to face conditions with respect to these transient unemployed men. There was no way in which they could get relief, and what we were trying to do was to bring the matter to the attention of the government in order that something should be done. The same condition obtains to-day. I do not believe for one minute that farmers are influenced by sentiments of self-pity: suggestions of that kind have no relevance so far as they are concerned. Although I myself represent an urban constituency, I am sure that the farmers around the city of Toronto and north as far as lake Simcoe have at this time one matter in mind, and that is the winning of this war, but they do say that it is pretty difficult for them to make a living at the prices which now prevail. The whole idea of this resolution was to try to obtain constructive suggestions from hon. members as to how, in the words of the motion, you can-
. . . create a parity of prices as between agricultural and other products in order to improve the condition of Canadian agriculture and in
Supply-State of Agriculture

order that it may receive a just and fair return, and thus be enabled to make that contribution to Canada's war effort which is so desirable, and which our agricultural population so greatly desire to make.
That is what the farmers whom I know want-some kind of aid.
As to the subamendment which was moved by the hon. member for Weyburn (Mr. Douglas), from my point of view and that of my constituents, it has some merit; also there are some points about it which I do not care for. On the whole, I feel that I shall have to support it, although there are a couple of things in it with which I do not agree. It seems to me odd that we should be paying some people not to produce, and paying them, too, at the rate of $4 per acre. I have no doubt that there are farmers in the northwest who would be very glad to dispose of part of their farms for $4 or $5 or $6 an acre, and yet they are to receive $4 per acre for summer-fallowing; to my mind it does not quite make sense, especially in a time like this, when we do not know what the future, particularly with respect to Europe's food supply, will be. When the war is over there will be, so far as I can see, a period of starvation or of famine in those overseas countries which will be terrible, and it seems to me that we ought to carry on and produce, not pay people to do nothing.
There is another consideration which appeals to me in connection with this whole wheat policy. Each year as we come back to the house we have the same kind of discussion; there is always the question of how much we shall have to pay in the form of a bonus or something of the kind. What is the difficulty? It seems to me that the government has not had any policy which has lasted more than a week or ten days at a time. Much the same applies to these regulations; every ten days or so new ones are brought out. It would be much better were we to get into mass production of wheat. It is the only industry in Canada which is trying to compete and which is not on a mass production basis. If, say, a group of half a dozen farmers out there have not sufficient equipment, why should not the government help them out by supplying them on a cooperative basis with the tools and equipment which are necessary to enable them to produce in competition with any others? Having done that, there must be something else they can do: they could be employed elsewhere for the remainder of the year. Coming from Ontario, I feel that we must try to do something for the people out west, and especially in Saskatchewan where they have had a pretty tough time. Really it is not their own

fault; a number of other circumstances come into the case, and we must help them out. But something more constructive must be found than this business of bonusing them each year. It is not good enough; they do not want it. I know that farmers in our part of the country are not very keen about bonuses; they want to stand on their own feet. There must be some scheme of helping farmers out west to operate in a cooperative way, and of employing, the remainder of the year, in other occupations, those who are unable to do mixed farming or carry on upon their farms the year round.
As regards the subamendment, the only thing which worries me a little about it is the proposal to levy 50 cents per bushel as a processing tax. If it will make any serious increase in the price of bread I do not think it should be adopted; for we should try to keep the cost of consumptive goods at the levels we have them at to-day. However, I understand that the processing tax would add to the local cost of manufacturing a loaf of bread not more than somewhere between three-quarters of a cent and a cent. That is not very much, calculated over a year. I am looking at this question only from the point of view of my own people. If it is going to help the western farmers by providing them with a little more money for their wheat, I feel that, under the circumstances of to-day, I shall have to support it.
With respect to the proposal to make further provision for storage, that is along the lines on which I have been talking, namely that we should continue to store up wheat even though we have to finance the operation. The point is, let us produce it as cheaply as we can. We must store it so that we shall have it when the war is over.
So far as this resolution is concerned, I think it has been a splendid thing to have the benefit of the discussion and advice from all quarters of the house. I would not have spoken on this question if I did not feel so strongly about it.

subtopic: SUSPENSION OF STANDING ORDER 28 THIS DAY TO PERMIT DEBATE ON MOTION OF MR. ILSLEY FOR COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
subsubtopic: AGRICULTURE-AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the terms set out in the
six paragraphs included in the amendment to the amendment moved by the hon. member foir Weyburn (Mr. Douglas) are so unusual that I could not be content with registering my opposition by a simple vote.
Before quoting these six paragraphs, I beg permission to call your attention to what I consider as a mistake in the first line of the second paragraph of the French translation. The English reads as follow's:
That a processing tax of 50 cents a bushel, etc.

Supply-State of Agriculture
Here is the French translation:
Que la taxe de transformation de 50c., etc.
It seems to me that the English text has not been followed closely enough and that the French should read:
Qu'une taxe de transformation . . .
I now quote from page 2319 of Hansard, session of 1941:
1.	That the minimum price for the 1941 wheat crop be set at 85 cents per bushed, basis No. 1 at Fort William.
2.	That a processing tax of 50 cents a bushel be levied on all wheat processed for consumption in Canada, the proceeds of such tax to be added to the minimum price of 85 cents a bushel.
3.	That the delivery of the 1941 crop be made on an acreage quota, such quota to be determined by the storage space available during the crop year 1941.
4. That the government of Canada make advances to farmers for the purpose of providing funds with which to build essential farm storage.
5. That the government of Canada make provision for advances to farmers on the credit of the quota to be delivered.
6.	That the government of Canada maintain and carry the wheat surplus as an essential part of its war policy.
I want to point out that the imposition of a fine of 70 cents on each barrel of flour bought (15 cents a bushel) is a very poor way of acknowledging the efforts made by the east t.o put the west on its feet; the injustice and ungratefulness becomes overwhelming in this last suggestion of increasing the fine by raising the tax from 15 cents to 50 cents a bushel, that is, $2.25 a barrel of flour, and besides, to request that it be levied on all wheat milled for Canadian consumption.
The terms set out in the other paragraphs are just as improper and unacceptable.
I dare hope that this amendment, which does not originate from the government, will not be carried by the house, as the present tax is unwarranted, and the amounts so far allotted to the western *wheat producers by parliament are out of all proportion to those granted to other provinces or their various producers. However, it is appropriate to point out that the ever increasing demands of the west become more and more unbearable, especially when the hundreds of millions of dollars that have been voted for their benefit of late are taken into account.

subtopic: SUSPENSION OF STANDING ORDER 28 THIS DAY TO PERMIT DEBATE ON MOTION OF MR. ILSLEY FOR COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
subsubtopic: AGRICULTURE-AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I know I shall be forgiven for taking a little of the time of the house to discuss the important question of agriculture, one of the main reasons being that from the year 1921 to 1931 we had in northern Ontario, particularly in my own section of the province, the greatest agricultural development that has taken place
anywhere in Canada, greater than in any other section of the dominion. I am interested in land cultivation myself. Although northern Ontario is well known for its mining activities, there runs from the province of Quebec westward to Manitoba a wonderful stretch of land known as the northern Ontario clay belt, 700 miles long by 60 miles in width, covering nearly 42,000 square miles, and comprising one of the finest farming lands anywhere in the world. We all realize that to-day Canada is facing a peculiar situation for a country its size. The reason is that, so far as new agriculture is concerned, pioneering will cease within a few years. I mean that we have gone as far southward as we can go; and so far as Quebec, Ontario, the three western provinces and British Columbia are concerned, the day is not far distant when we shall find it impossible to go farther north for farming owing to climatic conditions.
In our section of the country, by reason of our geographical situation, we have always taken a national point of view of agricultural problems in Canada. We are always in sympathy, and we try to work in the closest cooperation, with eastern farmers; and the same applies to the farmers of British Columbia and the three prairie provinces.
Coming to the present motion, which is a vote of censure against the government, I have no criticism to offer. I have 'been long enough a member of this house to realize that it is part and parcel of our so-called parliamentary system. It is very much like the private members' day, which gives a certain amount of leeway to the private member to express his views on different problems that are before the country and, in particular, his own constituents. Personally, I think it is the best way of bringing as forcibly as possible to the attention, both of the house and of the country, the various problems that affect different sections of the community.
As regards the subamendment, I have no quarrel with it for the reason that it falls practically into the same category as the amendment itself. But I do suggest that it would be a splendid gesture if hon. members refrained from taking a vote on these motions, because by the time this debate is over the purpose of the amendment and the subamendment, namely, a thorough and lengthy discussion of the agricultural problem, will have been fully served. The problem is not a new one. It is as old as the world itself. The agricultural problem has always faced every nation in history, and the trouble has been more and more accentuated during the last fifty years, or at any rate the last forty years. It is pretty much like our railway
Supply-State of Agriculture

problem; it has to face new situations. Agriculture is facing a situation which is not of its own creation or volition, but it is a situation that must 'be faced just the same. The problems that affect agriculture are constantly changing; they change so rapidly that it is impossible for any government, federal or provincial, to have a cut-and-dried policy to deal with them. We must solve them gradually and as they arise.
An lion. MEMBER: It is purely a money question.

subtopic: SUSPENSION OF STANDING ORDER 28 THIS DAY TO PERMIT DEBATE ON MOTION OF MR. ILSLEY FOR COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
subsubtopic: AGRICULTURE-AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
More particularly in
connection with agriculture. One of the greatest causes of unrest leading to the present European war has been the position of agriculture in various countries, and the trouble cannot be remedied overnight.
I think it is to the credit of the members who have taken part in this debate that they have contributed their talents and their knowledge to the discussion of the problem with a view to bringing its gravity to the attention of the Canadian people. Farmers from the east and from the west, from every section of Canada, have stated their views, and though some hon. members may have been a trifle partial, nevertheless I believe they all realize the impossibility of legislating on the wheat question or agricultural problems generally to the satisfaction of everyone concerned. It is absolutely impossible. For instance, I would be the last one to doubt the sincerity of the hon. member for Portage la Prairie (Mr. Leader). He is a practical farmer who knows what he is talking about, and speaking in all sincerity he says that last fall he told the government what it should do with regard to the wheat policy. But member after member from western Canada stood up and expressed views different from those of the hon. member for Portage la Prairie, and they were just as sincere and just as determined as he was to have the question settled. They are as anxious as the hon. member for Weyburn (Mr. Douglas) to bring about a solution of the problem.
All hon. members therefore will realize how impossible it is for any government dealing with this important question to satisfy all those who are affected by adopting all their viewpoints. But there is one common ground on which we can all stand, and that is cooperation with the government. I have given that cooperation in the past, because I believe this country has been blessed with a number of able federal ministers of agriculture, such as Doctor Tolmie, Mr. Motherwell, Mr. Weir and the present Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner)

I am speaking only of those I 
have known personally. The province of Quebec is also blessed with a premier who is well versed in agriculture, being a farmer himself.
The premier of Ontario, Mr. Hepburn, also knows the aspirations, the ideals and the problems of the farmers, not onW in Ontario but also in the west; and I believe that several of the western provinces have premiers who are very well versed in the problems of agriculture. So that as far as that is concerned we are on common ground. I sat in the opposition for a number of years, and I never doubted for a moment that the government of that day was sincerely trying to solve the problems that faced agriculture then. Some people may say those problems were not solved. That is true, but if was because they were incapable of complete solution. We must be logical and practical in our approach to these matters. I believe it is up to the farmers, through their representatives, whether provincial or federal; it is up to the agricultural associations and up to the nation as a whole, to make sure that the sentiments of the farmers are voiced, because after all the safest foundation for any country-and this applies particularly to Canada-is the agriculturists, the primary producers.
Anyone who has read or given any study to the Sirois report will 'have noticed how careful those gentlemen were to endeavour to -make the Canadian people familiar with the so-called western economy. To-day it ill behooves any member, whether from the east or from any other section of Canada, to criticize the government in regard to any money that may be spent to assist the western farmers. The opening of the west was of great assistance in maintaining unity within the Canadian confederation. It 'has permitted the Canadian people to widen their geographic and national horizon. We must realize at the same time, however, that the fathers of confederation and later the railway builders considered that the whole economy of western Canada of necessity must be based on the growing of wheat and other grains. They thought, as we thought until a few years ago, that Canada was really the granary, the bread-basket, not only of the British empire but of the civilized world. At the present time, however, we are facing new economies, both industrial and agricultural. To-day our western farmers are experiencing something similar to the disturbances which were experienced in Great Britain at the time steam power was invented, and when electricity was being developed. Only twenty-five years ago in my part of the country, when we were still in the pioneer stage, when there was practically no land cleared in that wonderful clay belt, we were paying as much as $40 or

Supply-State of Agriculture
$50 a ton for bad hay from this part of the country. Now we have an abundance of hay, with no market for it beyond the local consumption or in the raising of dairy cattle and horses. If our chemists and scientists could turn our grain and hay into oil and gasoline we would have no grain problem at all.
We must face these things as we find them. Time and again members of this parliament have stated that farmers, both in the east and in the west, are practically industrialists. They do not use horses; they use tractors, trucks and automobiles, and this is only right. I remember all the trouble we had only a few rfiort years ago with regard to road construction in northern Ontario. There was a time when the construction of colonization roads in the north enabled our settlers, using horses, to earn extra money during the slack season, but only a few years ago the contractors began to use trucks. Our farmers held all sorts of meetings in various parts of northern Ontario deploring the change and asking the government to use horses only. I took it upon myself to hold several meetings with the farmers in my part of the country, at which I told them that they must accept the change that had taken place throughout the country and realize that it was no longer possible to use horses only in connection with road construction. To-day most of our farmers are themselves using trucks and tractors. Whether or not it is a good thing I do not know, but they must keep up with the changes that take place in other parts of the country and face things as they are.
That is why I say that in dealing with the problems of agriculture we must be indulgent and broad-minded in our approach. We must take the point of view that is taken by the farmers of to-day, not that which was taken by the farmers of ten or twenty years ago. So far as agriculture is concerned we have built up an artificial economy and an artificial civilization throughout the world. I say that because in the past we have helped our industrialists, our manufacturers, and to some extent our financiers, without at the same time helping the farmers. Perhaps that was the right thing to do; personally I do not believe it was. In any case during all those years we thought it was possible for the farmers to stand on their own feet. But when you help one section of the population, from either provincial or federal funds, of necessity you must at the same time try to find a solution to the problems facing agriculture; and that is why I do not at all fear the result of bonusing, or whatever you may call it, the farmers or helping them directly from the federal treasury. I have always felt that when we were helping 14873-156
our industrialists or our financial men we should have done the same thing for our primary producers.
To-day the world is facing a new situation. Undoubtedly it is true that we have overproduction so far as wheat is concerned; and since the growing of wheat and other grains is practically an industry in Canada at the present time we must deal with it as we have dealt with our industrialists in the past. In other words we must curtail production, even though this may be against all the laws of nature. There is no doubt that some curtailment of our wheat production is absolutely necessary. The same statement applies just as forcibly to farmers in the east and in northern Ontario when they find themselves with no markets for their hay and other products. In my own constituency I have seen 200,000 tons of first-class hay which you could not even give away. Should we keep on producing more and more hay for which we can find no market? The answer is obvious. The day has come when the economy of the west must be changed from the economy of twenty years ago. Western Canada must have a greater population, though perhaps not many more should go on the land. They must work out a self-sustaining policy, and I believe the step being taken by the government at the present time is a move in the right direction. Oh, I know some eastern farmers feel uneasy when they visualize the time when western farmers may go into mixed farming more extensively; but if that day is to come there is no use in trying to delay it any longer. It is up to us in the east to adapt ourselves to that condition. I say a move of that kind is absolutely a step in the right direction, because it will help the western farmers to realize that they cannot keep all their eggs in one basket, that they must have diversity of production, which is found in every other country in the world.
It is true that this wheat question has not been created solely by this war. We suffered from these difficulties for some years prior to the war; but we hope that when this horrible conflict is over every bushel of wheat in this country will be required to feed the people of Europe. However, we must profit by our experience after the war of 1914-18. At that time we thought European agriculturists could never compete with our western farmers in the growing of wheat, but we saw countries like France, Italy, Germany and many others subsidize the growing of wheat rather than buy it from Canada, thus building up a false economy, and we may have the same situation when this war is over. There is always an element of danger in interfering with the laws of nature, though nature herself is also



Supply-State of Agriculture
wasteful. I say that because I do not believe we should build great hopes, so far as the wheat market is concerned, for the time when this horrible conflict will be over; yet it may be the other way round-wheat may save mankind from starvation.
If anyone will take the trouble to study present industrial statistics he will readily realize that the west is going more and more toward industrialization, more and more toward the development of its natural resources. No doubt we will hear more about a national coal policy, and I hope it will be possible in Ontario to use more Alberta coal than we do at the present time. Using more and more of our own natural resources will help not only people in eastern Canada, but those in the west as well.
Sometimes we in the east become a little impatient with so-called political eruptions in the west. We have seen the development of the Social Credit party and other progressive movements. If an easterner takes the trouble to study those developments thoroughly he will find there is a reason for such political and economic eruptions. We may describe as fallacious and dishonest such things as debt repudiation in the west, but I suggest we cannot throw them out as easily as that. We must look into them more thoroughly. We must study social credit and its cause in our political life, approaching it from the western viewpoint, the reason for its flourishing; and always remembering that it is the policy of one of our great western provinces. The same reasoning must be applied to debt repudiation and other political movements of the last thirty-five years.
I want to believe and the Canadian people want to believe that the people of western Canada are just as sincere and honest in their opinions as we are in the east; and I say to their credit that they have certainly been vocal in their expression of them. If through their legislation they find it necessary to repudiate certain interest payments on their debt, then I say it is not up to us immediately to condemn them. We must study the situation; we must learn why in their primary industry of agriculture they are suffering. We must learn what the farmers of Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba have suffered. The farmers in my section and in other sections of Canada have not made great profits, but certainly they were living more comfortably than were the people in some sections of western Canada.
Again I make an appeal to my eastern friends. I know they are open and broadminded. They do not want an east and a west; no, we do not want that. Without trying to moralize, may I say that I listened

carefully to what the hon. member for Portage la Prairie had to say. Although I represent a mining, industrial and agricultural constituency, I want to represent every section of the population in Canada. When I took my oath of office I took it as a federal, a national member. I must give my best study not only to the matters affecting my own constituency, but also to national problems which may have to be faced at any time.
This is the duty which confronts also our western friends. I would be the last man to try to moralize or to make any effort to discipline members from the west, but I would ask them, too, to be fair in regard to the agricultural problems of the east. They have studied the problems confronting the eastern farmers. They realize that many farmers in the east are working under heavy mortgages. Some hon. members might be astonished to learn that during the depression years in my own section of the country nearly eighty per cent of the farmers were on relief. Some of them, of course, should not have been there; they had no right to be there. But the majority on relief had to be there, so as to keep body and soul together. I mention these matters so that western members, appreciating the fact that we in the east have problems to face, will the more readily realize that acrimonious and partisan discussion in parliament on this all-important question would seem to be out of order. In other words the Canadian people will not tolerate at this time political discussion in connection with the great agricultural problem. I believe that agriculture has benefited in the last few weeks from what has been said by the Minister of Agriculture and by hon, members from eastern and western Canada.
Perhaps the farmers may blame themselves for part of the problem they have to face. Labour has found it possible to form unions- unions and organizations which were absolutely necessary. The more labour is properly unionized, the better it is for labouring men individually and collectively, and the better for the nation as a whole. Farmers are great individualists-so much so that it is unlikely they will ever organize to the point where they will get the things to which they are entitled, or as labour is organized. If it were possible to have an organization of the farmers from one end of Canada to the other dealing with their individual and collective problems, I believe it would be one of the finest and most practical ways of approaching them. Generally speaking, however, farmers from my section of the country will have practically nothing to do with those from southern Ontario. In my constituency we tried to organize

Supply-State of Agriculture
a settlers' organization. We worked for years and years, going into all kinds of smaller settlements, holding meetings, telling the settlers in our section of the country that for their own sake and for the sake of northern Ontario they must of necessity organize, outside of any political affiliations. At one time we had hope of success, but after two or three years of struggle we had to give up.
Why was that necessary? It was because of the intensive individualism of the farmer. Some time, however, they may realize the necessity of uniting themselves, so that the nation may be fully seized of the problems they are facing. It would not be wise for any hon. member unduly to criticize the financiers or the big corporations for organizing. It is necessary that they organize in order to carry on their activities in the economic life of the country, and in this regard the principle which applies to finance and big business applies with equal if not greater force to agriculture.
I do not wish to deal at length with the wheat situation. I have never doubted for one moment the sincerity of the hon. member for Weyburn. In his subamendment he has made a modest request. It would have been just as easy to ask for $1.25 a bushel, and I believe most western members will say that would not have been too high a price to ask. He asks only for 85 cents. I am sure the hon. member for Weyburn fully realizes what the effect would be on the western farmers in his section of the country if the subamendment were implemented; it would not satisfy every one- far from it.
AYe knew that something had to be done, and the government has done it. Some may not regard the solution as a perfect one, but no human institution can always be perfect. I recall that when a few days ago the leader of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation *was speaking a question was raised by hon. members in the Liberal and Conservative parties. At the conclusion of this speech I sent him a note saying, "When you become Prime Minister you will realize how hard it is to please everyone." We all know that perfection is very difficult to obtain. Even the angels would find it hard to please every section of the country and each individual member.
This is why I repeat the wish I voiced a few moments ago as to withdrawal of the amendments wuthout vote. I know that each one of us is carrying in his heart and soul a heavy load. No Canadian or Britisher can be happy under present circumstances. The hon. gentlemen who moved the amendments must certainly be satisfied with the manner in which this discussion has proceeded. They must be satisfied, too, with the thoroughness 14873-156$
with which the agricultural problem has been discussed, and how sincerely and honestly views have been expressed from all sections of the house. I believe they would be doing a great service if they were not to ask for a vote of censure of the government. First of all it must be remembered that governments are human. Members of the cabinet would be the first to recognize that some mistakes have been made and will be made by this administration. But no good would come from taking a vote, I feel that such a procedure would be resented by the people. Some people ridicule the fact that the Minister of Agriculture and the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. MacKinnon) had to make amendments from time to time in the wheat regulations, but that in my opinion is only natural. They have repeatedly stated in the house that more amendments might have to be brought in, and this is an honest and practical way to proceed; it shows that they are open-minded. It shows how alive and alert the present administration is to the serious situation which faces western Canada.
I do not like to throw any bouquets, but I believe the present Minister of Agriculture is the best man we could have for his position at the present time. We have great respect for him in our section of the country, we appreciate the extent of his experience in agriculture. We know that he wants to solve not only the problems of the western farmer but also those which face agriculture in general. I know he has been working in all sincerity, I know he has been taking advantage of all the advice which has been offered with a view to introducing legislation which will be helpful to our western farmers. This legislation will not solve all their problems; that it is humanly and physically impossible to do, but to some extent it will alleviate their condition at the present time.
I was grieved a few days ago to read an article written by a former member of this House of Commons for whom I have always had the greatest respect. She was asking the farmers to go on a sit-down strike because their present situation is so deplorable, because they are not as prosperous as they used to be. This is not the sort of thing that leads to national unity. Our labour unions are not advocating that labour should go on a sit-down strike. As I know labour unionism, it is ninety-nine per cent loyal and patriotic. There is a place in the internment camps for those who comprise the small minority which is opposed to our fighting the battle of civilization and preach subversive ideas and agitation in labour ranks. I repeat that the farmer will not go on a sit-down strike. No one is more loyal or patriotic. The farmers do not
Supply-State of Agriculture

want to be coddled, but at the same time they feel that their representatives have the right to express their views in this house as forcibly as possible to the end that they may be able to live their lives as they should be entitled to live them, that they may be in a position to support our national activities to a greater extent than they find it possible to do at the present time.
I do not want to enlarge any more upon this subject; it is one of considerable magnitude and could be discussed at great length. It may be a revelation to hon. members to know what is the true state of affairs in connection with our eastern grain growers. I have been in this business in the past. I have also been a dirt farmer, and I have no greater pleasure during my leisure hours than to get behind a plough. For many years I have been a grain dealer, and I believe I speak the truth when I say that southern Ontario has no surplus of these grains.

speechtext:
I do not think southern Ontario can supply all our requirements. Every time we have needed a carload of coarse grain we have had to get it from Winnipeg or some other point in the west. I believe that only about ten times during the last twenty-five years have I been able to get a carload of coarse grain from eastern Canada. Some people seem to be afraid that the western farmer will go into the growing of coarse grains as extensively as he has gone into the growing of wheat. I am not afraid that that situation will develop. After all, the western farmer is a realist. He knows that there is no money to be made from growing too much grain, and he will not do it.
Bonusing is something of which we should not be afraid. We have bonused to a certain extent our apple and tobacco growers. Many times in this house I have heard hon. members ask that greater restrictions be imposed upon the importation of fresh fruits and vegetables from the United States. I should like to say a few words on this important matter.
Ninety per cent of the sulphite and newsprint production in my section of the country is sold to the United States. Every day a trainload of newsprint leaves the mills in this district for the United States. Every ounce of the gold produced in the Porcupine, Kirkland Lake and other districts of northern Quebec goes to the United States.

subsubtopic: AGRICULTURE-AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I know of one mine in which there are 25,000 small stockholders, so that they really belong to the people. On this question of fruits and vegetables, we shall always be in sympathy with the southern Ontario farmer, but it must not be forgotten that the moment restrictions are placed against the importation of fruits and vegetables, we in northern Ontario will have to pay through the nose. We shall be ready to do that if it is helping our people in southern Ontario. There are fine highways into northern Ontario, and as soon as our own district is able to produce fruits and vegetables trucks by the dozens and hundreds enter the district from southern Ontario and flood the domestic market. We do not want to criticize this practice; these fruits and vegetables come from southern Ontario and we realize that the southern Ontario farmer must live, but some of our farmers are penalized by it.
If restrictions are placed upon the importation of fruits and vegetables from the United States we must consider the position of the 200,000 people gainfully employed in our gold mining industry. What will happen to them if we cannot sell our gold to the United States? What will happen to the pulp and sulphite exports from northern Ontario and Quebec to the United States? What will become of the market for our cattle, to which the hon. member for Portage la Prairie (Mr. Leader) referred the other day? We must take a national view of these matters. I am not an easterner or a westerner, I am really a central Canadian. I know what is going on in the west and in the east, and I shall always be willing to dig down, with all I have, in order to help the farmers of the west or the east. I am ready to do that in order that our farmers throughout the length and breadth of this country may be satisfied.
You cannot plan for a static solution of our agricultural problems. We must face new situations as they come up from day to day. The fathers of confederation never visualized what would happen to our present extensive system of railroads. Who would have thought twenty-five or thirty years ago that the buses and trucks would have taken so much traffic away from our railroads? Even such an experienced railroad man as the late Sir Henry Thornton did not believe that this would happen. Speaking in North Bay a few years ago he said that the more automobiles and trucks we had on our highways, the more traffic there would be for our railroads. But that prophecy did not come true.
Agriculture is facing a new situation in the dietetic propaganda which has been put forth throughout the country in recent years and

Supply-State oj Agriculture
which will have to be counteracted by our bakers and wheat growers. Because of this propaganda the consumption of wheat in Canada has diminished by fifty per cent per capita in the last fifteen years. After reading the propaganda put out in our daily and weekly press by so-called dietitians, I am almost ready to believe that if I eat too much bread I will be poisoned. Western civilization has been built on wheat eating. As water will eventually work its way through stone, so has this propaganda had its effect upon the consumption of wheat. We have been led to believe that citrus fruits are absolutely necessary and that if we eat too much bread we will get indigestion or our health will be permanently injured. Only six months ago the bakers in Ontario started some counterpropaganda and I understand that this has proven most beneficial, not only to the bakers but also to the wheat growers of the country.
I repeat that agriculture in all civilized countries will for many years to come have many problems to contend with which cannot be fully solved but which any parliamentarian who understands his mandate must endeavour to understand with a view to bringing forward measures that will assist in alleviating the present situation of the farmer, and so that the country will be seized of the exact situation. Everybody will admit that agriculture has been seriously neglected in the past, with the result that there has been built up what is largely a false civilization. This must be rectified. We hope that in a very few months or years from now, when our boys will be coming back victorious from the battlefield, it will be possible at least for those of them who lived on the farm prior to enlisting to go back to the land, and they will go back if their fathers and relatives and friends who have been occupied in farming during the war are comfortable and fairly prosperous. But it would be impossible to drag them back to the land if the farmers were then facing conditions such as they had to face during the great depression. Our agricultural problems are not easy of solution, but they deserve serious study and for many of them at least a partial solution can be found.
Here in Canada we are standing on the highway of the civilized world. If we envision the future that lies ahead of us we shall be able to build up a country which will be great, not only industrially but agriculturally, because we all realize that a large part of our population must of necessity find their occupation in life in the primary industry of agriculture. We shall thus build up in this country a balanced economy and our citizens
will be proud and happy to be Canadians and Britishers and to do their utmost for the advancement and welfare of the nation as a whole in a world that may well look for leadership from our privileged and beloved land.

subtopic: SUSPENSION OF STANDING ORDER 28 THIS DAY TO PERMIT DEBATE ON MOTION OF MR. ILSLEY FOR COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
subsubtopic: AGRICULTURE-AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have followed with a great deal of interest the debate thus far, and I hope that every farmer member of the house will make his contribution to it because, goodness knows, there are not many of us here. So I hope that every farmer member will exert himself to speak in this debate.
I rise because I can no longer sit quietly in my seat knowing as I do the state of mind of the average farmer and the effect which it may have on our war effort, particularly if Japan enters the war and food supplies from Australia and New Zealand are cut off from Great Britain. Canada would then be the source of supply for the mother country.
What do we find? Our farmers are both dissatisfied with the future outlook and disgusted with present farm policies. In other words, they have lost faith in the federal government because there is no medium between the farmer and the government. The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) has let us down either because he is no longer interested in our problems or because he has too many other responsibilities. What we most urgently need is a minister of agriculture who will spend his full time in looking after the interests of the farmers. Farmers are planning to carry on their operations on a limited scale owing to the high price of labour, and they are not planning to produce to the maximum because they can see no light in the present inequality between agriculture and industry and labour. This is a calamity, because industry and labour cannot and will not be able to contribute their fair share to our war effort without the farmers.
During the war of 1914-18 a great majority of farmers had a reserve of cash and feed and they were appealed to from patriotic motives to buy victory bonds and to increase production of food products such as wheat. They responded nobly. The farmer is a patriotic and a noble man if given an opportunity. In this war the reaction has been different; farmers cannot purchase war certificates or war bonds or war savings stamps. The reason is that he has not the therewithal,, and he resents finding himself in this position. Naturally, he lays the blame on the federal government for having forgotten him in the drafting of the war policy of this country. Agreements have been entered into by the Minister of Agriculture without giving the farmer any consideration. He is forced by
Supply-State oj Agriculture

labour shortage and price to discontinue production. He feels that the British people should not be aspect to pay more, but he also feels that the difference should be made a national responsibility, to be taken, if you will, from the revenues of the federal government, so that armers may not be asked to sacrifice more than other groups in the country.
There is also the feeling throughout the country that the war effort has bogged down at Ottawa. The farmer feels that the Minister of Agriculture is playing party politics along with his leader. This should not be in war time.

speechtext:
These are my notes and I am making the speech. I have been in this house for some time now and I have not interrupted any member making a speech. There has hardly been a member opposite who did not read his speech in this debate, and the only reason I am sticking to my notes rather closely is that I have not had the educational opportunities that most lawyers have enjoyed.
What we need is to produce efficiently more supplies for our army and to equalize matters between the various groups so that all will share and share alike in the endeavour to beat the common enemy. What we need is the confidence and unity of the Canadian people in doing what is required in this war effort.
To give a concrete suggestion, we all know that the dairy industry is a major industry in this country and that butter, condensed and evaporated milk and fluid milk prices are influenced by the price of cheese. We know that Great Britain wants 112 million pounds of cheese from Canada in 1941, and more if possible. The solution seems to me a simple one, and if the Minister of Agriculture wants to do something, the facts are plainly before him. Farmers are not so dumb, but they just cannot keep on producing at a loss. They must have sufficient income to defray expenses and live, if nothing else, and I contend that this government must bolster up the morale of our rural
IMr. Cardiff.]
people if it expects to get the maximum war effort. An increase in the price levels will spur the farmers on to pile up the cheese figure, and that in turn will be reflected in the cream producing industry. The small bonus which the Minister of Agriculture has promised is just like a bone to a hungry dog. It satisfies only for the moment. Why cannot we have a minister who will forget politics in these trying times and give agriculture the attention it deserves? The farmers are waiting for the Minister of Agriculture to come down to earth. Instead of floating along as we are we should be producing to the maximum.
If Japan gets into the war and Australia and New Zealand are cut off from sending supplies to Great Britain, Canada will be required and should be prepared to meet the demand that will arise. We would be in a nice position if we were one year late in our endeavours! If we were allowed to send our surplus to the nations which are now in need we would have a ready market for all we could produce. Dumb as the Minister of Agriculture may think we are, price will be the factor in deciding how much and what products the farmer will produce. Give the farmer a reasonable profit on his main products, his dairy produce, beef, hogs, eggs and grain, and he will pay higher wages to his help and be a steady purchaser of war bonds and war savings certificates and stamps.
The morale of the rural people at present is at a low level. Something has to be done to raise it. The federal government has failed and failed badly so far to promote unity of purpose and effort in the war need. The Minister of Agriculture has lost the entire confidence of the average farmer. Coming from a rural riding and knowing the condition that agriculture is in, I insist that speedy action be taken before it is too late. There is a limit to the endurance of the farmer. There is not a shadow of a doubt in my mind that unless a change is made for agriculture, seventy-five per cent of the farms in Canada will be mortgaged for all they are worth. It will not only cripple this generation but will tend to cripple the next generation as well.
There are a few things I should like to know.
I should like to know from the Minister of National War Services, now that we no longer have an active minister of agriculture, why we farmers in Ontario have to pay $24 per ton for screenings. I understand these screenings are taken as dockage from the western farmer after he has paid the freight on them to the head of the lakes. They do not cost anything when they get that far, and yet when they get down to Ontario they cost us anywhere from $20 to

Supply-State of Agriculture
S24 per ton. I contend that we should be able to buy those screenings, plus freight and handling charges from the head of the lakes, anywhere in Ontario.

speechtext:
Then I should like to know why the price of fertilizers has been allowed to increase to the amount of $12 per ton. I find after some study that we have a monopoly in Canada of sulphate of ammonia. Sulphate of ammonia is a by-product of the steel industry in coking plants. It supplies the cheapest form of nitrogen the farmer can buy. All other sources of nitrogen rise and fall according to the price of sulphate. You can readily see, therefore, the viciousness of an ammonia monopoly to the farmer. Canada is producing more steel and steel products to-day than at any previous time in her history, and consequently we have more sulphate of ammonia available. Instead of its costing S12 per ton more to-day it should be cheaper if we had a minister of agriculture who was interested in the farmer's welfare.
There is no question in my mind that there are a great many different ways in which the minister could help the depressed farmer besides pegging the price of wheat, bacon, cheese, butter, et cetera. We have heard a great deal from the government members about unity. How can any country have unity with forty per cent of her people in the condition in which we find agriculture to-day? Unity has not to do with the difference between English and French-speaking people in Canada. Unity means the equalizing of all groups in Canada regardless of race or creed. We have French farmers in Quebec suffering just the same as we are. Don't let this Liberal government pull the wool over your eyes any longer. We have heard enough of this farcical unity talk. What we need is comparative prices; nothing else will satisfy. We are getting sick of everything being bolstered up at the expense of agriculture. What we need is a minister of agriculture who will fight for the rights of agriculture. I lay the responsibility at the door of the Prime Minister. He is the one who is guilty of keeping a minister who is of no use to the farmer. Why does he not appoint a minister of agriculture who would at least take some interest in the welfare of the farmer? It would create more unity in Canada by far than this so-called political drama that has been going on between the French and English, or Quebec and the rest of the provinces. This government has no constructive policy so far as agriculture is concerned.
Let us face the facts. I contend that, if this government had faced the facts, we who are agriculturists would not now find ourselves in the deplorable condition in which we find ourselves at present. How can we have a united Canada, a united war effort, a united anything for that matter, so long as we are labouring under these conditions?
If this government just keeps on ignoring agriculture as it has in the past without giving a thought to our future welfare, we who are English and French, or descendants of any other race, will soon be able to supply the true definition of unity in Canada. We will most certainly disregard the political aspect of the set-up.
According to a statement made by the Minister of Agriculture in his address on Wednesday, March 26, hogs had decreased in value to the extent of less than 50 cents per hundred under the last trade agreement, while the price received from Great Britain was $2.12 per hundred less than a year ago. This would lead one to the conclusion, either that the farmers are now getting too much, according to the agreement, or that they certainly did not get their fair share of the price received last year. Would the minister care to explain where the difference went, and who got the money?

speechtext:
I quote the hon. member for Victoria (Mr. McNevin) when he said, if we were assured by this policy that we would be able to buy cheap grain, it would not be so bad, "but we are not." We know from experience that feed such as screenings which costs less than nothing at the head of the lakes, by the time we get it down in Ontario, costs $24 per ton, or about $1.25 per hundred.
The minister claims that farm prices have improved slowly this last two years. Perhaps

Supply-State of Agriculture
so, but when we consider the price we have to pay for the things we must 'buy, the slight increase does not do us much good.
I should like to take just a few minutes to deal with the generous gift or bonus of $35,000,000 which is being handed over to the western farmer. I wish to deal with the matter in relation to the effect that it will have.
First, a very large portion of this bonus will go to those who are not in need and who have planned to make and are making the adjustments they are now being paid to make by this generous bonus of the government.
Secondly, the bonus in question will give very little help and very little assistance to the small producer of grain. It will force the grain grower of the west into the production of hogs, something he is not prepared to do or does not want to do unless he really has to. It will force him into an overproduction of coarse grains which will be hard to store and hard to get a profitable price for on account of freight charges. So far as I can learn many of these adjustments were being planned and would have been taken care of without such assistance; in fact I have been told that the western farmer never asked for any such bonus, and moreover did not want it.
You would have thought that the Saskatchewan government or the rural municipalities convention would have been the first to be consulted in regard to this new bonus before the Minister of Agriculture and the dominion government would have got into such a generous state of mind, but such was not the case. It came like a bolt from the blue without any consideration whatsoever being given to other parts of Canada.
The fact that the western farmer may be short of revenue, owing to his not being able to sell his wheat, will not warrant the throwing of 30 or 40 millions of dollars to the west without giving due consideration to the question where it is going or the effect it will have on Ontario or other parts of Canada as a whole.
I think the agriculture committee of this parliament should have been consulted in this regard. Here we have been sitting for over a year and the agriculture committee has never had one meeting. Has agriculture become of so little importance to this government that the committee on agriculture is no longer of any consequence? Surely the Minister of Agriculture has not become so efficient that he no longer needs to take advice on any matters pertaining to agriculture, or are the agricultural members in this house to be completely ignored? Surely the Minister of Agriculture should be the medium

through which we should be able to work out our many problems in a manner that would be at least satisfactory in part.
In conclusion, I suggest that we cannot expect much consideration from this government so far as agriculture is concerned, because when this debate started, or fifteen or twenty minutes after it started, only fourteen members out of 180 on the government side were in their seats.
