I hope I shall not be accused of reading my speech. I shall endeavour to get along without reading too much of it.
Before dealing with the subamendment, I should like to review the situation with reference to this motion, which came before the house first on March 26, following an announcement by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. MacKinnon) and the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner). I think the house will agree with me that at that time the hon. member for Haldimand (Mr. Senn) and I, as real dirt farmers, simply wished to have a general discussion, a fair, unbiased and reasonable discussion, on the great problem affecting agriculture to-day, a problem which at the present time is second in importance only to the war. On April 7 the Minister of Agriculture wished to bring before the house, prior to the recess, his regulations with respect to bonusing and assistance to be given to the farmers. We agreed to withdraw the motion that night in order that the minister might proceed, on the distinct understanding that it would again take its proper place on the order paper the next day. I will not accuse the ministry of any deliberate attempt to have the motion omitted from the order paper, but the next day the order paper was printed without it. I make no accusation; far from it. However, as the result of some error the motion did not appear; and then, in order to have it.

reinstated-because it was understood that we were to have an opportunity of proceeding with the debate-it was agreed that two other members of the official opposition would bring forward the same motion. They did so, and we had to fall back upon two lawyers. In my opinion, they made a pretty good job of it. Now, however, there is a subamendment, and after having lawyers to plead our cause, we have had two preachers to pray for us.

Yres, but not as much as lion, gentlemen opposite do. He also did well, and I wish he would stick to his guns and support by his vote some of the things he said. We have also heard from other lawyers. Yesterday we heard from the hon. member for Halton (Mr. Cleaver). Well, he may be a pretty fair lawyer; but if he cannot do better at defending a client in a court of law than he did last night when pleading the case for the farmer, if I were in difficulty I would rather depend upon the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker).
Members on the government side have charged us with playing politics. I resent that charge, because when the motion was originally introduced we had the best intentions; we simply wished to have a general discussion of the whole agricultural problem, and in my opinion it was time for such a discussion. After the proposal was made to the house on March 12 by the two ministers, we heard from some Liberal members; the hon. member for Victoria, Ontario, (Mr. McNevin), the hon. member for Lambton-Kent (Mr. MacKenzie), the hon. member for Durham (Mr. Rickard), and the hon. member for Compton (Mr. Blanchette). One would have thought that these gentlemen would oppose the government in the proposal that has been brought down, and some of them came pretty close to playing politics in the statements they made; but it was just so much eyewash, because as soon as the government passed round the word to these boys that this was a want of confidence motion, they all ceased criticizing and fell into line. speechtext:
I was going to pay a
compliment to the Minister of Agriculture, if the hon. member would only keep quiet. Constructive criticism has never hurt any government, and I will be fair enough to the minister to say that in my opinion he would invite constructive criticism on this or any other subject relating to agriculture. He would appreciate such criticism. I know the manner in which he has received certain criticism out west, and I am frank in saying that he has received it with good grace, because I believe he wants to know what is wrong.
I recall a statement which the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Ross) made when he spoke. He went all over the lot and finally said that while this might not be the very best solution, if it were not a good proposal then it was up to this parliament and the public to devise something and let the government know. That is what we have been trying to do. Let me say this in fairness to the minister. The great difficulty in which this or any other . government finds itself, when dealing with a problem of this magnitude, is the lack of information, knowledge and understanding on the part of those who are directly affected. That is a difficulty which is common to all governments in a matter of this sort.
While at times in this house, in carrying out what I deem to be my responsibility as a member, I have been critical of the government-and not only of this government but of the government which I had the honour to support-I have always tried to offer constructive suggestions, and I have the satisfaction now of knowing that when criticizing the government for its inaction with respect to this problem I offered in 1938 a suggestion which, since then adopted, the Minister of Mines and Resources (Mr. Crerar) ridiculed at the time as moonshine-storage on the farm. I was the first man to propose a processing tax and the principle was adopted by the present Minister of Trade and Commerce and put into operation. I also suggested the quota system which this government has employed. I take satisfaction, therefore, in the fact that while I have been critical I have at the same time offered something worth while which has been subsequently accepted.
It may be true that on March 26 I was critical of this proposal which was brought forward by the two ministers; but I did offer a suggestion as to what the government should do, and I venture to suggest that if this war continues, my proposal will be accepted within a year. I have before me an editorial which appeared in the Winnipeg Free Press, making some comments along the lines of my criticism. I said this action was too drastic,
Supply-State of Agriculture

in bringing about the reduction in one year; I referred to the quota system, and this editorial states that had the quota system been in vogue for a number of years we would not have the problem we have to-day. On February 2, 1934, I proposed that the quota system be adopted. Unfortunately I could not sell the idea to my own government; but certainly if that suggestion had been accepted, we would not have been faced with such a huge surplus as we have to-day.
I think the minister will agree that this is far from being a solution of the problem, that it is only a temporary measure. Before dealing with the proposal in detail, however, I should like to make one or two other observations. I think we will all agree that western Canada's wheat 'is Canada's commercial life-blood, and I believe maintaining the price of that wheat on a parity with what the producer has to pay for those things that go into wheat production is the concern of every Canadian and certainly should be the concern of every member of this house. That was what our proposal meant, in the first place. In considering this problem there are two main factors to be remembered. First we have the production end; we have the farmer who tills the soil, does the seeding, harvests the grain and delivers it. Then we have the physical handling and marketing of that grain, which I believe is equally important in the economic life of the western producer. That being so, if we are going to ask the producer to grow that grain, not at cost plus but at cost and, in many instances, at less than cost, it is our duty as members of this house to see to it that the physical handling and marketing are not carried out on the basis of cost and a tremendous plus.
I think every fair-minded man will agree with that statement. This government has done little or nothing to deal with the second factor; it has allowed the grain trade to make a large profit.
We as a parliament have a duty to perform. The Minister of Trade and Commerce made the statement that we have $400,000,000 invested in wheat; and under present conditions that wheat is practically as good as gold.
I wish the hon. member for Rosthern (Mr. Tucker) were in his seat at the moment, because I believe he would agree with what I am now going to say. Having $400,000,000 invested, the government is in the wheat business for at least a few years; so I believe this parliament should amend the finance act or the Bank of Canada Act or some such act in order that sufficient currency might be issued on the security of the wheat held by the board to finance the whole project, so that no interest charges would accrue on the 
money invested in this wheat. That may be a step towards inflation, but I venture to say that in a short time we shall come to that also.
I have another suggestion to make. In the circumstances, with the government in this business, I think they should take control of all human-food grains produced in Canada, whether manufactured or not. That would put a crimp in some of the profit now being made on some of the products of agriculture.

Mr. PERLEY': I did not know about that. I say that there is confusion, and that the minister has confused us even more. After his double-barreled announcement of February 12, an order in council was passed on April 2, another one on April 8, and now another one on April 30. Then, when he was out west he sent a telegram, a copy of which I have in my hand, but which I shall
Supply-State of Agriculture

not read. He stated what applications should be in, and advised secretaries of municipalities to organize, and to advise farmers to make their applications before the first of May. That confused all of them.
I might add that I tried to help a few farmers. I attended three meetings, and addressed them. There was confusion in their minds, and I helped them as much as I could in reading the recommendations and regulations as we then had them. We have now a different set, and we have no indication that it is final. I say that because I have before me, in the minister's handwriting, these words, "This may be the final"-he hopes- "with a few minor changes." I say that there will be confusion right along. The government may think they are right in going through with this proposal, but I say that they will destroy the soul of western Canada before they have finished.
Yesterday, when the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Graydon) was speaking with respect to advertising products and by-products of agriculture, the minister suggested that the hon. member should read the press to see how those products have been advertised. I hold in my hand an advertisement published under the authority of the dominion Department of Agriculture. In it I find the following:
Help Canada win the war by growing less wheat in 1941.
Get your application completed by May 1, 1941, if possible.
What did that cost? It appeared in practically every western paper, and I suggest that it will be fine fodder or dope for Hitler, when he hears that we are encouraging the farmers to grow less wheat, in order to win the war. It is not long ago that we heard Lloyd George on the radio state that Britain's greatest need is food. Yet we have the government saying, "Grow less wheat in Canada to help win the war." The two statements are conflicting, to say the least.
It is not too late for the government to adopt the subamendment. If the government were prepared to adopt it, I would ask that they accept, too, the suggestion I made on March 26, that for the duration of the war- and I would make it longer, if I had my way- the government should take over all storage facilities in western Canada and operate them for the benefit of the producer.

Why do I say that? I believe I can prove that if the government set the price at 85 cents, there would be no loss on the 180,000,000 bushels exported to Great Britain. I hold in my hand a chart dated April 26, 1941, setting out a monthly review of the wheat situation. At page 6, I find the heading, "Liverpool wheat offers, f.o.b. port of shipment, March 1940 to date, (Canadian cents per bushel)". This chart shows that from March, 1940, to April 26, Liverpool has been offering over 80 cents for Canadian wheat in Canadian ports on the St. Lawrence, and Saint John. The chart shows that in the last two months, namely, March and April of this year, Liverpool has been offering 89 cents for No. 1 Manitoba at St. Lawrence ports.
The Minister of Trade and Commerce issued this chart on April 26, and I should like to ask him if it is correct. Why did he publish it and give the impression to the people throughout the west that since April, 1940, the government have not sold a bushel of wheat at less than 80 cents? That is what this chart says they have been offered. If they did not accept the offer, what excuse have the government? If the minister wants to answer now, he may.

cent price covered by the subamendment of the hon. member for Weyburn (Mr. Douglas). I was showing that the government could do this and yet have no loss because they have

not sold a bushel of wheat to Great Britain in the last year for less than 80 cents. I was sticking to the amendment. Further, the minister, or rather the member-he will be a minister in the government some day

the hon. member for Weyburn, mentioned the processing tax. I have stated that there would be no loss at 89 cents. He cut his name off, but the firm name can still be seen. This is the card setting out the prices. What is going to happen? We will wait and see.
After my statement wais made in the house on March 26, I received many letters from and had many interviews with different people. I have received letters from California, Vancouver, the city council of Port Arthur, and many others stating that I was on the right track. I have in my pocket a telegram from a member of the Winnipeg grain exchange asking me to meet them. I did meet them and they told me, "Perley, from a patriotic point of view you are right, and it is time the government had the courage to take hold of this thing and stop the racket."
I have a letter here from a grain man. It is from California. I have his name here in his own handwriting. He says:
When reading your debates on the floor of the house relative to the government taking 
over all storage grain elevators, I wondered if the Canadian government elevator at Port Arthur is still leased to the McCabe Grain Company with head offices in the United States.
I have not time to read the whole letter, but the writer goes on to say:
This elevator has a storage capacity of 3,250,000 bushels. ...
At two-thirds of a cent a bushel per month for storing grain, the company is drawing down $260,000 a year from the dominion government. That is for storing wheat in an elevator owned by the dominion, an elevator leased for $51,000 a year.

I wrote to the chairman of the board of grain commissioners in Winnipeg asking whether McCabe Brothers have the government terminal elevator at Port Arthur under lease, and, if so, what rental they paid.
I have in my hand the letter I received from the board of grain commissioners. I shall not read it all because it is too long. The gist of the letter is that -the elevator was leased to McCabe Brothers in 1930 or thereabouts, and the lease was renewed in 1938.

Supply-State oj Agriculture
The first rental was by public tender; the lease went to the highest bidder, which was McCabe Brothers, and the price paid then was $45,000 a year. On August 1, 1938, there was drawn up by this government or by the board of grain commissioners a new lease running for a period of six years with a minimum rental of $51,000 per annum, and the lease was given to McCabe Brothers. The rental had, therefore, increased from $45,000, which was the highest paid before, to $51,000, and the letter of the board of grain commissioners states:
The increased rental was designed to pay off during the continuance of the lease the cost of additional cleaning machinery installed by the board.
There is $51,000 a year paid for leasing an elevator which, if full, with 3,250,000 bushels of wheat, would return $260,000, and I presume that the elevator is full. I could give twenty other cases almost as bad. Now, with a war on, and when the people of this country are to be asked on June 2 to subscribe to a victory loan and with the budget that was introduced here the other day, will any member who is in favour of the government continuing to do this sort of thing rise in his place and show himself to the house?

That is what I say. There is not a member who dares to rise in his place and say that he is in favour of the government continuing to do this thing, and I could give twenty other cases almost as bad. There are 3,000 annexes or more, and some old elevators built forty years ago for $10,000, which are earning $2,500 and $3,000 a year. The government should take the whole thing over for the duration of the war; if this were done, there would be a saving of $40,000,000 a year which should be added to the price of wheat paid to the farmers, and it would not cost the treasury o-ne cent.
I have here a statement of the elevators which I would be glad to put on Hansard if I had the time. In conclusion, Mr. Speaker,
I say that this is a human problem and it requires a big man with a big heart to settle it, a man with initiative, courage, and ability to inspire and do the right thing. The people of Canada are beginning to realize what is going on; and if the government do not take some such action as I have suggested, they will be remiss in their duty. Thousands of people in western Canada know what the situation is to-day; and if the government take the proper action, they will have little trouble in raising the amount required for their victory loan in June. The elevators in western Canada are paying from 25 to 80 per cent on their capital investment, and they are full of wheat. There never was such a racket before. The government should take over the whole thing for the duration of the war. If this matter had gone to a committee of nine members, where sworn testimony could have been taken and witnesses produced, we would have got the facts and appropriate recommendations would have been made.

Oh, yes. In my opinion it is perfectly possible to avoid it. The object of moving such an amendment on such an occasion is to give hon. members from all parts of Canada the opportunity to ventilate this question for the benefit of the farmers. It gives opportunity for the expression of opinions which hon. members have received from the farmers in their ridings and enables the matter to be debated with the hope that out of yet one more discussion of this farm trouble some beneficial methods or alterations of present methods may be adopted.
Following the introduction of the amendment, there comes a subamendment. I have little doubt that the views expressed in the subamendment represent the views of the farmers in the riding of the hon. member who proposed it. While I have no intimate knowledge of the fact, I assume that the views expressed by that subamendment are also supported by the farmers of many other parts of Canada. It surprises me, therefore, that neither the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner), nor the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. MacKinnon) nor any spokesman for the government has given an expression of the government's views on that matter. It is true that a few moments ago the Minister of Agriculture excused himself, shall

I say, from making such a statement because, when we get into the estimates on agriculture, he will have his opportunity.

subsubtopic: AGRICULTURE-AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Before the coming of the subamendment. Since the moving of the subamendment the minister had every right and all the opportunity he required to make a governmental statement on the subject. It is not a matter of grave moment to me personally so far as my constituents are concerned, because in my forthcoming remarks I cannot deal principally with wheat. I do, however, draw attention to this fact, that a vote of some importance will be taken shortly, I presume, without any statement of government policy with regard to the matters raised in the subamendment.
This is an opportunity which hon. members have of ventilating this old, old question of the difficulty which faces the farmer in the marketing of his crop. It is not confined to Canada. It is not confined to the British empire. It is a worldwide problem; it is always before us, and maybe it cannot be too often debated. There are difficulties inherent in each branch of agriculture. Certainly there are difficulties inherent in t'he marketing of wheat. It has been said in this house that the difficulties which the wheat producer faces to-day are those produced by the war. I have heard it stated by those who in my opinion are well versed in wheat matters that, had the war never occurred, this wheat marketing problem would have been right before us in Canada to-day and in all the other wheat-producing countries of the world. It is a problem which will have to be tackled, lest destitution and misery come to all that section of farming Canada which is dependent upon grain for its livelihood.
There are portions of agricultural production which certainly are affected by the war. Difficulties have crept into the marketing of those commodities which particularly are associated, even in part, with the export market. Apples are one. The dominion government, very properly I think, has recognized the marketing of apples as one thing which is affected as a war casualty, and has entered into certain arrangements in the last two years, including this one, with those two provinces which are principally affected by the export of apples. It is a perfectly proper arrangement that the taxpayers' money on this occasion should be used for assistance

in this matter, as it has had to be used in the assistance of other people in Canada who have suffered as war casualties. The difficulty -which we are looking at once more is that of closed farms, empty barns, and all those sights which are not only saddening but demoralizing to the people of Canada, whether they are intimately connected with agriculture or not. We are looking on at farmers' sons who so infrequently remain on the land that it seems as though they are ready to try any other walk of life rather than that one in which they have been brought up, and in which they have seen their fathers working long hours, at very hard work, for pittances on which they have endeavoured to raise families.
Those are the difficulties that confront the generation which is coming along, and I know of no more lamentable instance than the inability of farmers' sons to remain on the land and make an adequate living. It is a particular difficulty, which we must tackle. If we do not tackle it; if we do not find some hopeful solution, even in part, those who come after us will most assuredly blame us.
I am sitting in this house as the representative of a constituency in southern British Columbia which, with the exception of mining in the southwest corner and in certain other spots in the riding, is almost wholly given over to agriculture. Besides those who are in a primary way busied in agriculture, there are all those in the secondary industries intimately connected with agriculture, those in professional life, those in business, and those in a secondary way are dependent upon the success of the farmer. I have lived there for thirty years, and in that time, and for, I dare say, ten years before that, there have been many, many attempts to tackle successfully this question of the marketing of produce.
The southern part of the riding is largely given up to the production of fruit. Two-thirds of the riding is given up to the production of vegetables and fruit, and the remainder of it is largely concerned with dairying and forage crops, with three areas, comparatively small in size, in which the grains are grown. I know it will be said that they are such minute areas as to be scarcely worth considering in the measure of the prairie provinces. Yes, there is some truth in that. But let it not be forgotten that, to the farmer who grows that grain, it is just as important to him, whether it is grown in the constituency of Yale or in one of the constituencies of Saskatchewan. It is also not without interest that just to the north of Vernon in the Okanagan valley there is a farmer, a Scotsman, who three years ago grew and marketed

Supply-State of Agriculture
ten thousand bushels of Marquis wheat, all of which graded No. 1 hard, without any dockage for weeds or foreign matter; and that same Scotsman the year before grew and marketed fifteen thousand bushels of wheat which graded No. 1 northern. I believe that hon. members from agricultural ridings will agree that this is a pretty satisfactory record, from whatever part of Canada it comes.
The main difficulties with which the farmer has had to contend have been the problems connected with the marketing of his produce. The cooperative efforts of the last thirty years have followed the usual course of cooperative efforts. They have succeeded; then the faith in them has dwindled; then a terrific year of marketing has come, and cooperation has benefited once more. But there has always been this trouble, that those who were ready to cooperate, to form a cooperative union, had to leave out those farmers who had no intention whatever under any circumstances of cooperating with their brethren, with the result that the umbrella which was laboriously raised and held over the market of this perishable product was taken advantage of by those who did not intend at all to cooperate but who, with perhaps comparatively small quantities of produce, were able to jump into and out of a market and get rid of their produce, leaving behind them a wholly demoralized market in which large volumes of produce still on the hands of the producers had to be sold. It was not wonderful, therefore, that gradually the idea got about that cooperation by itself, based on the voluntary acts of farmers, was not likely to succeed, and pressure was brought to bear on the provincial government with the idea of endeavouring to obtain marketing legislation which would place in the hands of the farmers sufficient power to enable them to carry out the orderly marketing of their produce.
On three occasions the provincial government of British Columbia passed such marketing measures, and on three occasions those measures fell by the wayside after trial, after they had been made use of, because of the old difficulty of the constitutional question as between what the dominion government and the provincial government can properly control. Eventually, therefore, we arrived at the time when there was in office a dominion government that was ready to proceed with a natural products marketing act, which would aim at overcoming that constitutional difficulty. Since I wish to deal for a few moments rather connectedly with that measure and what happened to it, I should be grateful, Mr. Speaker, if you would call it six o'clock.
At six o'clock the house took recess.
After Recess
The house resumed at eight o'clock.

subtopic: SUSPENSION OF STANDING ORDER 28 THIS DAY TO PERMIT DEBATE ON MOTION OF MR. ILSLEY FOR COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
subsubtopic: AGRICULTURE-AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
At six o'clock, Mr. Speaker, after having made a few preliminary observations, I was advocating the re-creation of marketing legislation, because I am firmly of opinion that under certain circumstances and for some crops there is the probability that considerable assistance may be given the farmer when trying to remove the obstacles in his marketing path. There is one great difference, I think, between the marketing of farmers' crops and the marketing of other commodities. Three things may happen to crops. They may be sold when they are ready for market; they may be stored, at considerable expense, or they may be destroyed. Therefore there is everything in favour of some control which will induce the orderly marketing of these perishable commodities.
The bill that was introduced into this house during the session of 1934 met with a stormy reception. Every conceivable allegation, contemptuous and inaccurate, was levied against that measure by the then Liberal opposition. From the present Prime Minister down, there were things said of this measure which certainly its authors did not recognize as facts. It was said that it was unwarrantable governmental intrusion into business. It was said that the government could set the prices of field crops. It was said that it was regimentation; and with one honourable exception the whole Liberal party went against that marketing legislation. That honourable exception was Hon. W. R. Motherwell, one time Minister of Agriculture, who put his principles above his party. Because he believed that this legislation would provide some solution for the farmers' difficulties, he supported it; he took part in a useful, critical examination of it on the second reading of the bill, and he voted for the measure. That bill received royal assent early in July, and by the middle of September twenty-one boards had been set up under it.
Let me point out what that legislation set out to do. It meant just this, that where in a given area a sufficient majority of the producers of a certain crop were desirous of joining together and electing a board which should direct the marketing of that crop, they should be permitted to do so. A petition could be sent to the Minister of Agriculture, who would examine the situation in the locality concerned. If he were satisfied that a prima facie case for control had been made out, a poll was held; and if a sufficient majority of producers were in agreement with the setting up of a board, that board was set up.
Supply-State of Agriculture

By the middle of September, as I have said, twenty-one boards were set up in this country: six for fruit, five for vegetables, three for fish, three for milk products, two for tobacco, one for jam and one for shingles. The very first board to be set up was the British Columbia tree fruits board, which handled the fruits of the Okanagan valley and the surrounding territory. The headquarters of that board were in Kelowna, in my constituency, and I therefore took a close interest in its setting up and subsequent work. As I shall show in a few moments, that board met with such success that it has continued in existence all these years, although the act under which it was originally set up was later destroyed.
I pointed out that marketing legislation was not entirely new in this country, that there had been provincial legislation. This, of course, was restricted in its character, for it could control only the sale of commodities within the borders of a province. The difficulty arose when the produce of one province was being marketed in other provinces; and it was to overcome that difficulty that the federal act was passed. The principle underlying the federal act was just this, that if it were desirable to have this marketing legislation, there should be a federal act, and that parallel with that act there should be provincial acts. The provincial act could control the marketing of the crop within that province, while the federal act could give the same measure of control to the sale of that produce in the other provinces.
Seven of the provinces set up provincial acts. Obviously it was convenient that the same board should be accepted under both the federal act and the provincial acts; and in the case of the British Columbia tree fruits that board proceeded to carry out its arrangements, not in selling but in directing the sale of all varieties of such fruits. The course that board followed was to issue licences to those shipping houses then in existence which were prepared to cooperate with the board and do its bidding. During that year and into the next year satisfactory results were obtained under this control of sale. Tor one thing it was possible to prevent that undercutting by the man with but a small quantity of produce to sell, the invariable result of which was the smashing of a market. It prevented the marketing of immature fruit, one of the most serious drawbacks to the fruit industry of this country, because there are so few parts of Canada which honestly and honourably support the fruit act in the matter of grading. It also prevented one variety of fruit from being rushed on to the

market before an earlier variety had been cleaned up. All those matters were handled by that board in a way which had never been possible while there were a dozen or a score of shipping houses all selling as and when they might.
But the government changed; and the new government-with vindictiveness, I am sorry to say-decided that this act must be destroyed. Appeals to the government were made in number, not only by Conservatives, to permit the supreme court to examine this matter in the way that courts are accustomed to do such work; that is, not to have the act pitched at the court, saying, "Here; is this good or is it bad," but to have a case brought regarding an infringement of the act, so that the matter might be gone into in the way that lawyers and judges are accustomed to do their wmrk. But no, they were adamant; they were going to destroy that act, and the act was thrown to the supreme court. The counsel who was employed to present the case in all probability was a most worthy professional man, but certainly he was not conversant with this type of legislation. The case of the parallel provincial act which was interlocked with the federal act was not plainly described to the court. The supreme court threw the act out. The next step was that the government decided it would go to the privy council. It went to the privy council, and the privy council upheld the finding of the supreme court. As a result, the act was dead.
But the judgment of the privy council made curious reading for those who had followed this piece of work consistently through its various stages. Naturally it was a matter of intense interest to those in British Columbia who had thrown in their lot under the board which was set up under the act. I was rather taken with the words used by a prominent fruit grower in my neighbourhood who, having read and studied the judgment of the privy council, made this statement: "The privy council seems to me to be saying, 'if you had presented this properly, our decision might have been difficult, and possibly different; but in the form and on t'he facts presented we have no difficulty in arriving at a conclusion, and we are much obliged to you for helping us out of rather a tight corner'
Whether that be a true and accurate description of the finding of the privy council in this matter, I do not know. That is a matter for a lawyer. But I do know this, that whereas the support for this marketing legislation in Canada might have been measured at that time in hundreds, I would say that to-day the support for such legislation might be measured by a thousand, or many more than a thousand. Judging by the corre-

Supply-State of Agriculture
-spondence, judging by utterances, judging by resolutions, judging by articles in the press, if you will, I believe there is an acceptation widespread among the farmers of Canada that until they can be given some power within their own ranks to control their own marketing, they will always be dependent upon the whim and will of the selfish one, usually one with but a small quantity of produce to sell, who can undercut the market, decimate it and leave it as one in which the bulk of the crop will have to take its chance.
It appears to me that if the government were to see fit to tackle this marketing problem along lines similar to the action previously taken, and were to grant marketing legislation, they would do something for which they would receive the gratitude of the Canadian farmer. I believe also that the Canadian farmer would be honest enough to remember and to recognize the courage and foresight of the Right Hon. R. B. Bennett, who, with his Minister of Agriculture, the late Hon. Robert Weir, was responsible for the presentation of the legislation to this house. I believe the farmers would do well to forget the type of criticism which was used at that time, and which dealt with this legislation as an unwarrantable intrusion into the lives of our citizens; for, Mr. Speaker, you cannot drive your car down Sparks Street when the traffic lights are against you. Is that not restriction of the liberty of the subject?
It has been said that man, from the cradle to the grave, is having his liberty controlled by this regulation and: by that piece of legislation. Why is it being done? It is done because we live in a democratic country, in a country where the rule of the majority holds sway. When it is obviously to the advantage of the travelling public that there should be traffic lights and rules of the road, and that there should be means of preventing the foolhardy from doing damage to the majority, the people of Canada and those of any other democratic country come in behind their governments, lay down regulations and pass laws controlling the liberty of the subject. We shall not overcome this marketing difficulty until, in a democratic way, we provide that the power to control can be given to the farmers when they, in sufficient majority, demand it.

subtopic: SUSPENSION OF STANDING ORDER 28 THIS DAY TO PERMIT DEBATE ON MOTION OF MR. ILSLEY FOR COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
subsubtopic: AGRICULTURE-AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think it desirable and fair not only to myself but to all hoe. members that before the vote is taken I should make my position perfectly clear. On former occasions I have tried to do so, and during the months this question of wheat acreage reduction has engaged the attention of parliament, the government, and the citizens of Canada, I have made my position fairly clear, I believe to most people. That is, I have said we have a surplus of wheat so huge that the nation dare not continue to add further supplies. I took the stand, and still adhere to it, that there was no course for the government to follow other than that of urging wheat reduction. I took the stand that if that were done, owing to the limited quotas the farmers would be allowed to deliver they should have a higher initial price. I have taken the stand that we should have at least another 15 cents a bushel, making a price of 85 cents, one which would really be less than the amount now being appropriated for .these so-called bonuses.
While visiting my constituency during the Easter recess, following my usual procedure I held some public meetings. On this occasion they were three in number. They were not just local meetings; they were held in districts where we have our largest population. At those meetings were gathered farmers from a distance of perhaps 15 miles. The meeting in Portage la Prairie, the largest centre in my constituency, was naturally a large one. After we had discussed the wheat reduction proposals, a resolution was passed, and I am going to read it to the house. It is dated April 19, and it reads:
The members of the Portage la Prairie local, Manitoba federation of agriculture, being opposed to the present government wheat policy offer this resolution as an alternative.
Be it resolved that the members of the Portage la Prairie local, Manitoba federation of agriculture, ask the dominion government to set the price of wheat for the first 230 million bushels at 85 cents, Port William, and let the farmers take what they can get for what they have left. Also forego any acreage bonus for summer-fallow or sowing of coarse grains or grasses.
There was also passed a resolution endorsing my stand in opposing the government's proposals. We had another meeting at Poplar Heights, which was also largely attended. A similar resolution was passed at that meeting and my attitude was endorsed by those present. Then another meeting was held at Warren, just outside Winnipeg. At this meeting, which was the largest of all, the following resolution was passed:
The following resolution was introduced by H. H. McIntyre and seconded by P. Beachell:
Whereas we realize the necessity of limiting the quantity of wheat upon which the government will guarantee a price of 230 million bushels, and whereas the suggested policy is unnecessarily complicated and difficult and expensive to administer, we submit that a guaranteed advance of 85 cents per bushel on 230 million bushels, with no bonus system whatever, would be simpler and would cost the government no more... Carried.
Supply-State of Agriculture

Moved by D. H. McIntyre, seconded by C. Cunnington: "That this meeting endorse the stand of Mr. Harry Leader in opposing the wheat policy as it stands now"... Carried.
I should now like to quote from a press release by the Canadian federation of agriculture, headed "Agriculture is saying." I may say that this is where the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) and I dare to differ. I took the stand that the Canadian federation of agriculture had suggested that a higher initial price be paid, and I contended that most of the rest of their representations were subordinate to this one. This was their vital suggestion; it was the essential point in the brief which they submitted to the dominion government. I quote from the subheading "Government policies blast farmers' hope," as follows:
When the delegation from the federation of agriculture met the Ottawa cabinet in January, it was highly commended by the Prime Minister for the constructiveness and reasonableness of its proposals and the fairness of its presentation. We were also told by the Minister of Agriculture that farm prices needed to be raised all along the line and that efforts of the government are designed with that objective in mind. We went home hopeful that a change in attitude and policy toward agriculture would be initiated without delay. We were hopeful that something would be done to remove the handicaps against agriculture and to give encouragement to Canadian farm people.
After waiting and hoping for two months, the government recently announced its new wheat program. And our hopes have been sadly shattered because that programme is disappointing alike to the farmers of the west and the east. It asks the western farmer to continue to produce wheat and sell a smaller quota of it at the depression minimum price of 70 cents a bushel. And it uses public funds to bonus the swing of millions of wheat acres into live stock and live stock products, which is bound to react to the disadvantage of the eastern farmer.
My vote must be in opposition to the government and in favour of the subamendment moved by the hon. member for Weyburn (Mr. Douglas). I feel that this is the only opportunity offered to me to make my position perfectly clear as we ring down the curtain on this piece of legislation which I feel must be designated as ghastly. The particular clause of the subamendment to which I refer reads:
1.	That the minimum price for the 1941 wheat crop be set at 85 cents per bushel, basis No. 1 at Fort William.
Speaking humbly, as a private member should, I wish to notify the house that I intend to vote for the subamendment.

speakeroldname: Hon. R. B. HANSON (Leader of the Opposition) :
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: SUSPENSION OF STANDING ORDER 28 THIS DAY TO PERMIT DEBATE ON MOTION OF MR. ILSLEY FOR COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
subsubtopic: AGRICULTURE-AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I had not intended to take part in this debate. I made certain

remarks with respect to wheat during the discussion of the estimate in connection with the bonus, at which time I referred to the demand for an increase in the processing tax to 50 cents a bushel. At that time my understanding was that such an increase would have a definite bearing upon the price of bread, which, after all, is the food of the poor man of this country. I felt that such a move should be barred, and I said so. Since then, the hon. member for Weyburn (Mr. Douglas) moved an amendment to the amendment of the official opposition, one section of which subamendment deals with a 50 cents processing tax to be added to an initial price of 85 cents a bushel, basis No. 1 northern at Fort William. I have been in accord with the subamendment with the possible exception of that one section. I made diligent inquiry, and I have learned that the price of wheat plays a relatively small part in the price of a loaf of bread. I have been informed that it amounts to only 14 per cent of the price, and therefore there should be no increase in the price of bread if a processing tax of 50 cents a bushel is levied against wheat for domestic consumption. This government has set up a board to prevent undue enhancement in the price of any commodity, and on one occasion this board has acted in connection with the present processing tax upon wheat. Believing that the government will use the machinery which it has to prevent the price of bread from being increased, I feel that I am now in a position to vote for the subamendment, and I intend to do so. I hereby declare my intention of so doing.
Having said so much, may I revert briefly to the whole question of agriculture. It may be thought that a professional man, such as myself, will have little knowledge of the agricultural problems of this country. I represent two counties in New Brunswick, one of which is wholly rural and the other more than two-thirds rural. I have lived all my life in that province, during which time I have been immediately associated with country people. That is where I was born and that is where I was brought up. During the long years of my life these men have been my chief associates. I have always endeavoured to take an intelligent interest in the problems of the farmers of my constituency. Without wanting to boast, and perhaps to my regret, I may say that I have probably more money invested in farms in York county than any other individual. It has been my constant endeavour to keep on the farm those young men in whom I have invested money. I intend to continue that policy until I shuffle off this mortal coil.

Supply-State oj Agriculture
I am interested in the farmers of my community, and on many occasions I have received a mandate to speak for them. That is my excuse for devoting a few minutes in discussing the situation in which agriculture finds itself after eighteen months of war.
In comparison with the tremendous importance of farming to Canada, the problems of the farmer, and particularly of the eastern farmer, have had relatively little attention from the government. It is trite to say that in a country constituted as Canada is, there can be no national prosperity and well-being, no all-out war effort, on the basis of a distressed agricultural industry, or an agricultural industry which does not receive a fair and reasonable share of the national income. Can it be gainsaid that to-day the farmer is in a distressed condition? He receives a much smaller portion of the national income than is his due. The result is that not only is he unable to participate as he would wish to do in the war effort through the purchase of war savings certificates and bonds, but in many instances, he is obliged to receive government assistance, which constitutes a heavy drain upon the national treasury.
There are many reasons for the situation in which the farmer finds himself to-day. The war has residted in the loss of many overseas markets. The surplus of farm products at home has depressed price levels, while at the same time war demands have increased the price levels of products which the farmer must purchase. That is a statement of fact which has been repeated in this house on man)' occasions and which no one will deny. Therefore, from the point of view of the legislators of this country, in aiding the farmer there is a vital and urgent need for a distinct aggressive agricultural policy to be pursued with vigour, resourcefulness and purpose by the whole nation. The present so-called agricultural policy of this administration is, to my mind, extremely vague and indefinite, and it has ceased to be a major factor in the national policy of Canada.
What is the record of the government in this respect since the outbreak of war? The answer to that question is not given by myself. It is found in the words of a friend of this government, a provincial Liberal cabinet minister, who is reported in the Ottawa Citizen, of February 12, 1941, as follows:
Without fear of contradiction, I say Mr. Gardiner betrayed the agricultural classes of Canada and left them to work out their own problems against insurmountable odds without any assistance from the Department of Agriculture at Ottawa.
The fact is 'that under the present minister the Department of Agriculture has given little or no direction whatever to the average farmer in eastern Canada. The farmer has not been advised how best he may coordinate his activities so that his production will be of maximum assistance to the war effort of both Canada and Great Britain, nor is there any prospect that leadership will be given by the present minister. He has too many jobs on his hands. How can he give direction to the agriculturists of Canada, run a wheat bonus policy and take care of all the national war services? If he can, he is a better man than I think he is.

subtopic: SUSPENSION OF STANDING ORDER 28 THIS DAY TO PERMIT DEBATE ON MOTION OF MR. ILSLEY FOR COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
subsubtopic: AGRICULTURE-AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
According to a Canadian dispatch from Regina appearing in the Montreal Gazete of January 24 last, the minister said-I want hon. members to listen to this; I hope the minister was not misreported:
An improvement in the economic position of the producer of agricultural products cannot be expected until this war, which we hope will not last longer than five or six years, is won.
Mr. Speaker, that is the counsel of despair given by the head of agriculture in Canada. If the defeatist attitude represented by these words of the minister is followed, it will mean that Canadian agriculture can survive only on the basis of peasantry.
The survival of agriculture as a national asset demands that this parliament, without delay, take the necessary legislative and other steps to raise the income of the farmer and at the same time to restrict undue enhancement of the cost of the instruments of production which he must of necessity purchase.
The normal approach to the solution of agricultural problems is threefold:	(1) by
the expansion and creation of markets; (2) by the reduced cost of production; (3) by fair and reasonable prices for farm products. I readily admit that at the present time no great hope can be held out for an increase of markets. Britain is taking what farm products she can, and no Canadian farmer is anxious to hold out on hard-pressed Britain.
Certain opportunities for expansion of markets exist in South America, and these should be explored to the utmost. I am glad to know that the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. MacKinnon) has, during the interval since last Christmas, appointed and sent to the south American republics an active young man from my own community to promote the sale of seed potatoes. I trust he will be successful. He has a rich field to work upon, and he can do a great deal of good. I commend the minister for what he
Supply-State of Agriculture

hag done, and I trust his choice will prove a successful one. But I do say to the minister that the trade mission which he sponsored last year should be resumed at the earliest possible date, and that the appointment of sales officials, whether they be trade commissioners or not, to south American nations should be proceeded with forthwith.
Immediate consideration should be given by the government to the suggestion which I made at the last session of parliament, and again during this session, that Canada should make a gift of foodstuffs to Great Britain.
To me, however, it is obvious that a solution does not lie in the expansion of markets but must rest in the reduced cost of production and the increase of return for farm products.
What is the situation to-day in Prince Edward Island? That little province, purely agricultural, is represented in this house by a minister of the crown holding one of the most important portfolios in the government, by an eminent gentleman from the city of Montreal, and by two local members. The plight and the problems of Prince Edward Island have never been given voice to in this House of Commons during these two sessions of parliament, and I wonder why. Be that as it may, let me tell the house that the farmers of Prince Edward Island have had an advocate in the person of the premier of that province. In a return brought down to this house on April 4, on the motion of the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Shaw), with regard to the processing levy on wheat, will be found two letters of great interest and importance. The first letter is dated December 13, 1940, from the premier of Prince Edward Island, and addressed to the Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Mackenzie King); and the second is dated January 2, 1941. I invite the house to listen to these communications: Charlottetown, P.E.I.,
December 13, 1940.
The Right Honourable W. L. Mackenzie King, Prime Minister of Canada,
Ottawa.
Dear Mr. King:
I find that there seems to be a considerable undercurrent of feeling among the farmers of this province, which is kept under the surface only by their intense political sentiment, but which may at a later date seriously react against their productive effort.
That is certainly a note of warning, and I hope that the Prime Minister and his colleagues, if they ever read this letter, will give some heed to it. If they do not, there will be some vacant seats over there after the next election. The letter proceeds:
Our farmers had no expectation or desire to receive the inflated prices of the last war, but 
they did hope to share to some extent in the improved markets resulting from increased wartime activity. _ They have therefore been greatly disappointed to find their situation worse this year than it has been since the trough of the depression. Prices of farm products seem to be going down, while prices of instruments of production, such as fertilizer, machinery, equipment, et cetera are steadily advancing, as well as the cost of such necessaries of life as the farmer requires to purchase. While there is not yet any scarcity of farm labour, it is becoming practically impossible for the farmer to procure, owing to the relatively high wages paid for labour on construction work. The farmer certainly cannot afford to pay anything like competitive wages with the present prices of farm products.

Yes, I agree that usually they are not able to do it. But I am repeating the remarks of the premier of Prince Edward Island, and my hon. friend has endorsed them.
Potatoes have been exceptionally low this fall and have been selling at little more than half the cost of production. Pork products, which the farmers claimed to be producing at a loss last year, have also gone down in price. The fisheries had an extremely bad year. The market for oats has been very low, although I admit that this feature has the compensation of inducing farmers to retain larger quantities of oats for home feeding. Dairy products have been low, with the exception of cheese, but Prince Edward Island has been practically out of the production of cheese for several years.
I believe that is true.
There now seems to be a prospect of improved prices for fox furs, but this does not benefit the ordinary farmer or fisherman, and in fact seems to add to their dissatisfaction. They cannot see the logic of rising prices in London for luxury products, while their lobsters are prohibited as a luxury, and pork products are pegged below their cost of production. This apparent anomaly is probably explainable by re-export or some such course of transaction, and it is extremely agreeable to the fox breeders of the island, but it only irritates the lobster fisher and hog farmer.
I am inclined to believe that these difficulties of the farmers will be automatically remedied to a large extent in the next year or two-
Well, that is wishful thinking, if nothing else. -as agricultural markets are always slower to respond to stimuli than industrial ones. The difficulty, however, is that the farmers of this province have entered the present phase only partially recovered from the effects of the depression. Many of them have already been forced under water, and I fear that the present adverse conditions will continue to force a great many more out of the productive field. Actual conditions will be greatly aggravated by the undercurrent which I have mentioned.
This undercurrent takes principally two forms:
(a) Dissatisfaction of the farmers at their present conditions as compared with that of other industries whose condition is greatly improved by the war programme;

Supply-State of Agriculture
(b) The feeling of resentment at the dominion overnment's treatment of western wheat armers as opposed to maritime producers.
It is, of course, very difficult even to suggest appropriate remedies for the loss complained of, and it is probably still more difficult to get the farmers to agree as to the benefits of such suggestions. There are, however, several points which seem to be universally agreed upon here, and which I may briefly mention:
1.	The potato market should be stabilized.
There should be marketing legislation such as that for which my hon. friend to my left, the member for Yale (Mr. Stirling), has pleaded.
It is, unfortunately, too late to do much in this direction for the present year. Nobody anticipated such a disastrously low price for potatoes in October and November, or steps would undoubtedly have been taken earlier in the season. The very farmers who needed assistance, namely those who had not the facilities or were not financially able to keep their potatoes, were forced to sell them in October and November at a ridiculously low price, and far below the cost of production and were thus deprived of any advantage from their principal cash crop. I am in hopes that the more prosperous farmers, who were able to retain their potatoes, will obtain a better price for them through the winter and spring. I should strongly recommend, however, that steps should be taken in good time for the stabilization of nest year's potato market.
I ask the minister to note that suggestion, and if it is now too late for this year, to heed it for next year.
This matter should be given early consideration, as it might possibly involve the giving of instructions in the spring as regards limitation of acreage. Probably a mandatory limitation would not be desirable, but the intimation should probably be given that a limitation would be put on the number of acres whose production would be stabilized.
2.	In regard to pork products, the farmers complain that they are obliged to produce these commodities as a war-time necessity at a loss on the cost of production. This being the case, they claim that the dominion government should accord them two forms of relief: (a) through the bacon board or some such agency the government should insist that the farmers of this province should receive a better price from the packers. There would seem to be considerable ground for this claim, owing to the contention that the prices paid at Moncton for goods to be shipped to Halifax are really lower than the prices paid for the same goods in Montreal. The purchasing packers in the maritimes seem to charge our producers up with imaginary transportation charges from Moncton to Montreal and return, instead of giving us credit for the actual savings in transportation;
I investigated that claim, and I believe it is substantiated by the facts, although I am bound to admit that I have not the proof before me to-night. But if that is so-and the Department of Agriculture can soon ascertain whether it is-it is a crying outrage on the producers of Prince Edward Island.
(b) that the dominion government should arrange reduced freight rates on the hog feeds which are necessarily imported to this province from western Canada.
I may say that so many conferences have been held on these points and so many maritime delegates have gone to Ottawa in the past year that it is difficult to imagine any way in which our claims can be more strongly presented. Apparently, however, no results have been obtained, and the disappointment and resentment of the farmers continues to smoulder.
3.	The alleviation of the wheat milling tax to the extent suggested by my letter would remove a considerable source of annoyance and indignation on the part of our farmers.
May I say that all of us, irrespective of political party, put our shoulders to the wheel, and we forced-I believe that is a fair term to use-the w'heat board to alter the interpretation of the statute. I am not going into that point at length, but they were only authorized to charge the processing tax on wheat purchases. Can anyone tell me that, when a farmer took his grist to a mill and waited for it to be ground, paid his toll and brought it back, that was a purchase? I threatened the ministers; I threatened the wheat board with an injunction. I did not have to go that far. The matter was not really of sufficient importance to take to the courts, but I believed that the rule of reason would win, and it did win. The position was quite unlike that in western Canada, where, I understand, there is a barter, which may possibly and probably be interpreted as a purchase. That little source of irritation has, after a good deal of struggle, been removed.
Here is the fourth suggestion of this Liberal premier of Prince Edward Island:
4. The farmers of the central and eastern portion of the province have been deprived of the expected benefits of the Wood Islands ferry, which would have given them a greatly improved transportation to the mainland, particularly for produce trucks. The province has cheerfully submitted to the loss of this service in so far as it was considered to be bona fide necessary war purposes. But, unfortunately, our people cannot be persuaded that the requisitioning of the two very ships which were provided for this service was altogether due to yvar necessities, nor has the procedure regarding compensation commended itself to those in this province who have been familiar with the detailed steps followed. After the requisitioning of the first ship, the provincial government felt obliged to come to the financial assistance of the ferry company, as this appeared to be the only way in which the second ship could be provided. The second ship was purchased with the full knowledge and approval of the dominion authorities, and seven or eight months and a great deal of money spent in reconditioning her, practically every step being taken in consultation with dominion departments. But curiously enough, just at the moment she was ready for service, it was suddenly discovered
Supply-State of Agriculture

that she was absolutely necessary for naval purposes. The resulting loss of the service and the seemingly unnecessary difficulties encountered in obtaining compensation have placed both the ferry company and the provincial government in an embarrassing position, which has not yet been resolved.
I should add that I understand it has been remedied so far as compensation is concerned.
Local enterprise has apparently been completely discouraged from any attempt to provide a third ship for the service, and in the meantime the only method of transporting produce trucks is by the Borden ferry, where exorbitant and almost prohibitive rates are charged.
I referred to this matter at some length last year, but that situation has not been remedied.
An agitation for the lowering of these rates has been carried on for many years, but without avail. I am inclined to think that the holding up of the Wood Islands ferry project is a strong argument for the reduction of the present exorbitant truck rates on the railway ferry service. I have no doubt that you would be astonished to learn the figures of the rates charged for ferrying even the slightest of trucks across the straits.
If the Prime Minister has any curiosity with regard to this matter, he will find that I myself put many of the facts on Hansard last year. The letter proceeds:

Business seems to be fairly good in Charlottetown-

The Prime Minister replied to that letter on the 2nd day of January, and at great length. I will not read the whole of the letter. He begins by saying that he has had an opportunity of discussing with his colleague "the representations of your letters of December the 13th", and "I propose to set out the position of the government on each of the questions you have raised."
First, he deals with the processing tax. That has already been dealt with. Second, he refers to the difficulties experienced by the potato farmers as a result of the poor market "this season". Then he goes on to deal with the situation in the United States, and he says, "It is difficult to see how low prices could have been avoided." Then he states:
The present surplus of potatoes, unlike that of apples, cannot be attributed to the effects of the war, since Canadian potatoes do not ordinarily go to European markets. Potato marketing problems are largely domestic, and it may be that some voluntary limitation of production might help, though experience would indicate that a reduction usually follows naturally after a season of low prices. Copera-tive marketing, of course, might offer some possibilities by enabling all producers to do the sort of orderly marketing that the more prosperous farmers in Prince Edward Island are evidently attempting.
Then he offers the service of officials of the federal department in helping to organize marketing machinery. He then discusses the question of hogs and so on, and winds up with a defence of the increases in fertilizers, discussing the law of supply and demand. This is his conclusion:
There can be only one satisfactory solution of the problems which face our farmers. That solution is the defeat of the aggressors and the destruction of the totalitarian order. No section of our community has so direct an economic interest in the defeat of nazi Germany as our primary producers of foodstuffs. That, alone, will make possible the opening of the channels of trade, and the restoration of

markets for our exportable surpluses. Without world markets, there can be no prosperity for our great primary industry.

During the Easter recess I had the privilege of holding a couple of meetings in my riding which were attended by every municipal official and by the officials of agricultural organizations in that riding. While some hon. members may not believe it, I endeavoured to keep the discussions non-political, pointing out to those people that the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) had said that this wheat reduction scheme was to be the policy and that we should discuss the regulations on their merits. I can assure him that many of those officials there who have staunchly supported this government protested whole-heartedly against the scheme.
Since my return to Ottawa, I have received from other municipalities in various parts of Manitoba resolutions commending the stand taken by the hon. member for Portage la Prairie (Mr. Leader) and by myself on April 4 in this house. Furthermore, the Minister of Agriculture stated on that same day that the farmers of the west knew that the policy was not putting money into their pockets but was making available for the treasury or from their pockets, an amount equal to $100,000,000, which would go to assist in financing the war effort at this time, or which they might have had were they treated on the same basis as other people in this country.
Anyone from the west will realize that these farmers had many difficulties in providing a livelihood and carrying on their affairs from the returns they received last year. I am sure I do not know what they will do this year on the reduced income-and the minister himself has admitted that it will be reduced. Moreover, setting the price of wheat at 70 cents under the scheme distinctly helped to reduce the price of wheat in the country. On March 13, the day following the announcement of the policy, May wheat in Chicago was only eight cents higher than the price of May wheat on the Winnipeg exchange. Yesterday the spread between Chicago May wheat and May wheat in this country was sixteen and a fraction cents.
This afternoon the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Perley) pointed out what was likely to happen in the near future; he said that farmers in the United States would probably receive a much greater price than it is proposed to pay our own producers. Hon. members will remember that when the President of the United States brought down his war budget in March, farm commodities were placed second on the list; and of that appropriation of some seven billion dollars, one dollar of every five was to be spent for the welfare of the farmers. Contrast that with the situation in Canada. We have voted an appropriation of some $1,450,000,000; and at the rate we are going now, we propose to spend only one dollar out of every $180 to help our farmers. That might be kept in mind, particularly in view of the repeated references by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley), when introducing his budget the other day, to what they were doing in Washington. It is not only we in western Canada who are having great difficulties. I have had the privilege of visiting many farmers other than wheat producers in other parts of Canada, and certainly the agriculturists of this country from coast to coast are up against a most difficult situation. We should endeavour to give agriculture greater consideration during the trying times that lie ahead.
I do not wish to take any more of the time of the house. I must vote for the subamendment, in the interests of my own constituents and of all the other people in the province from which I come, who otherwise probably will not have their views fairly represented.

The first section which is affected by that rewording is section 2.
2. (1) For the purpose of these regulations the wheat acreage reduction on any farm shall be computed by deducting the number of acres sown to wheat on such farm in 1941 from the number of acres sown to wheat on such farm in 1940.
That is, the first act which is necessary to the collecting of money under these regulations is that wheat acreage should be reduced. In order to determine what that reduction is, it is intended under these regulations that the acreage of 1940 shall be taken as the definite starting point. I should like to support what has been said by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar. Prior to the Easter recess I asked the minister if he would not consider amending these regulations along that line, and my trip home convinced me more than ever of the difficulty that I pointed out before Easter. In the drought area, not for only two years-if it -were -only for one year or two years one could take an average- but for a period of four or five years the total cultivated -acreage on most of these farms has been considerably reduced, and the wheat acreage has been drastically reduced. I knew there were odd cases like that, but when I went home I was deluged with them. A man came to see me and said he had four hundred acres under cultivation, of which only seventy acres were in wheat. Normally

that man would have 250 acres in wheat. A letter came to my desk this morning from a man who has 600 acres under cultivation, with only sixty-five acres in wheat. Normally he would have 300 acres in wheat. People like these did not reduce their wheat acreage because of the wheat surplus; they did so because for the last four or five years they have not had moisture, or have not had seed; or, if they had seed, they did not think it worth while putting it in the ground. They just carried on as best they could. These people will be penalized by this policy unless some adjustment can be made.
I think it was yesterday morning that I received a copy of a telegram which was sent to the minister by Councillor Keill -of Froude, Saskatchewan, which is in the Handsworth district where they are faced with this problem. It is not an easy matter with which to deal, but since in subsection 3 of section 2 of regulation 2 the minister inserted a provision that, regardless of whether a man has all -of his land sown to wheat, only eighty per cent will be assumed to have been sown to wheat, it occurred to me that this provision might also be reversed. Why should we not say that even if a man has sown very little wheat, perhaps only ten or fifteen per cent of his cultivated land, it will be assumed that thirty or forty per cent has been sown to wheat? If you are going to establish a maximum and say you will recognize only eighty per cent, no matter how much has been sown to wheat-and perhaps that is a good idea-why would it not be equally just to set a minimum? Why not say that a man who last year had only ten, fifteen or twenty acres in wheat will be assumed to have had thirty or forty per cent of his cultivated area, or whatever percentage the minister may consider fair? If, because of drought or lack of seed, a farmer's wheat acreage has dropped below thirty or forty per cent of his cultivated area, I see no reason why we should not set a certain figure below which he should not go. I hope the minister will consider something like this, because, if he does not, I know these people will lose any benefit they might obtain under this proposal.

If you start to draw the percentage higher than that and you let them deliver their whole quota on a certain acreage, you encourage those farmers who have only ten or fifteen acres each, to increase their acreage, and you will get far more wheat than you can take. In other words, the figures used the other night by the hon. member for North Battleford, I believe it was, when discussing the matter, are of some importance. It was stated that there are 9,000 farmers at the top who are growing so many thousands of bushels, and 17,000 farmers at the bottom who are growing a few acres of wheat. But that leaves out the 250,000 farmers in between. They are really growing the wheat. It is neither that small number of big farmers at the top nor that small group of small farmers at the bottom which is growing most of the wheat; it is the 250.000 farmers in between. You cannot bring down regulations
[Mr. Donnelly.J
to take care of that limited number of cases, without so affecting all that mass in between that you raise rather than lower the production of wheat.
You cannot settle all these problems on a basis of wheat alone. For example, a person in crop district No. 5, which is north of the Qu'Appelle river, gets from live stock an earning, based on each acre of wheat land, of $2.29. But down in the southwestern part of the province, the part about which the hon. member from Wood Mountain has been speaking, they get forty-nine cents an acre on their wheat acreage. The problem of solving one person's difficulty through wheat is entirely different from that of trying to solve the other one through wheat. The people who are in the area where there is mixed farming now are more likely to reap benefits from this policy than the people in the large wheatgrowing areas. They would just go on doing what they were doing, although they would do it to a greater extent than before. They will feed more hogs or milk more cows and get a little more money in that way; they will grow the coarse grains to feed them.
This whole question came up at every meeting which was held in the west. Some one would make the statement that he had reduced his wheat acreage. I agree that there must have been many people who 'have reduced their wheat acreages, but the number must be comparatively small when the whole picture is considered. Our total wheat acreage was increased last year by more than 2,000,000 acres. We had the highest wheat acreage in the history of western Canada, so the percentage of those reducing could not have been very high. I am informed

I have not Checked these figures myself, but they have been checked-that every single grain district in western Canada showed an increase in wheat acreage last year. There may be local situations where people have reduced their wheat acreages an unusual amount, but generally speaking that is not true. This will be found to be the case when the figures for last year's crop are considered.

I stated it to them in this way. If you want to make certain that you are going to have enough to make your delivery under the quota on the basis of twelve bushels on sixty-five per cent, take your whole acreage of last year and figure it at nine bushels to the acre. It puts the farmer in a position of being able to calculate somewhere near the amount of wheat he will be able to deliver next fall provided he gets a crop. If he does not get a crop he will collect on his reduced wheat acreage anyway.

Then there is this sixty per cent rule for 1940, and the rule of averaging would apply, so that his basic average would be thirty-five per cent. The hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Quelch) has been explaining the wheat policy on the basis of the remarks made by the Minister of Trade and Commerce in the house on April 8, and I have made an explanation along the lines suggested by the Minister of Agriculture. I am clear about his explanation. But at page 2269 of Hansard there is a table which the hon. member for Acadia placed on the record, and the Minister of Trade and Commerce, who I regret is not here to-night, made this statement:
I have seen the statement to which the hon. member refers; as a matter of fact, a copy was sent to me by the Calgary board of trade. I did not go into it very thoroughly, but I did read it, and I can say that the figure quoted with regard to the average yield of 25 bushels is correct. I have not compared that figure with other suggested or possible yields, but as I have already stated there will be a five-bushel
